Industry News: ICAO Hosts Air Transport Conference, Elects Upcoming Council Members

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Airlinegeeks

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, ICAO Headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where Member States and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection and sustainable growth.
  • It has been revealed that over 1,500 delegates from 154 Member States and organizations attended the week-long event thirteen years after the Sixth Conference in 2013.
  • “Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO stated in a press release during the Conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, ICAO Headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where Member States and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection and sustainable growth.

It has been revealed that over 1,500 delegates from 154 Member States and organizations attended the week-long event thirteen years after the Sixth Conference in 2013. They discussed high-level topics in commercial aviation: modernizing economic and legal frameworks, investing in infrastructure and skilled workforces, and ensuring that innovation keeps pace with rapidly changing technologies and global demands.

“Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO stated in a press release during the Conference.

According to recent reports, participants agreed on the value of frameworks that support innovation and investment for economic development. They stressed this especially for smaller landlocked States, which depend heavily on air connectivity for growth.

Recent findings suggest that the Conference supported modernizing air navigation infrastructure in line with ICAO’s Global Air Navigation Proposal. It also supported liberalizing air services agreements without making liberalization conditional on infrastructure development, since new air links fostered by more liberal agreements are seen as key to economic growth.

However, all initiatives should be flexible enough to address local circumstances and should not burden developing States. ICAO’s statement continued: “The Conference also reaffirmed that international standards are key to building effective, market-enabling policies and avoiding fragmentation that could impede cross-border air services. Delegates pointed to ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) as a successful example of this approach.”.

Participants were asked to express their views on the documentation proposing various initiatives with regards to consumer protection legislations that have become an integral part of the legal framework for all air operators.

It has been revealed that at the Sixth Worldwide Air Transport Conference in March 2013, ICAO was asked to develop Core Principles on consumer protection. The final document, adopted by the ICAO Council in 2015, contains provisions on:.

The report for the Seventh Conference invites States to modernize their consumer-protection frameworks, keeping them evidence-based, proportionate, accessible and responsive to the changing realities of commercial air transport. It also indicates legislation should establish clear responsibilities for carriers, intermediaries and other providers regarding information, complaints and disruption assistance.

ICAO is expected to review its Core Principles while preserving national and regional flexibility. It is also expected to assess whether existing policies adequately cover online intermediaries and other overlooked situations.

Many Member States cautioned against the ICAO Air Passenger Handbook proposed by IATA, because producing and maintaining a single repository covering many different national laws would be too costly.

The Conference asked ICAO to “examine the need for harmonized, risk-based guidance on the use of AI in aviation, including common terminology and meaningful human oversight.”.

According to recent reports, the rapid development of AI and its unknown effects on aviation operations is a topic Member States will need to monitor. ICAO will coordinate and facilitate international exchange, while States will oversee implementation to ensure that the technologies adopted are secure, interoperable and consistent with cybersecurity and data-protection objectives.

ICAO will handle AI within its existing structure, as the proposal to create an ad hoc unit was not supported.

During the final two days of the Conference, ICAO held an Extraordinary Session of its Assembly to elect the four additional Council members required by the entry into force of the 2013 protocol amending the Convention on International Civil Aviation. The Council is the Organization’s permanent governing body, accountable to the Assembly and responsible for setting priorities and implementing its directions. Its membership increased from 36 to 40, and there are no permanent seats.

Sources indicate that six candidates competed for the four fresh seats: Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Oman, Thailand and Türkiye. In the vote on the final day, Kazakhstan and Thailand were not elected, and the other four States won seats.

The Council now comprises Angola, Argentina, Australia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Oman, Poland, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States and Uruguay.

The next elections will take place at the General Assembly in September 2028.

  • While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused concerns for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

Recent findings suggest that this ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

Sources indicate that at Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:.

The problem is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:.

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”.

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

Industry observers note that while it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

In a recent development, ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the concern here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

Latest Update: The 5 Biggest Airbus A220 Fleets In 2026 Don't Even Include The Jet's Launch Operator

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Air France took delivery of its 60th Airbus A220-300 on November 6, closing out a five-year narrowbody renewal program.
  • The budget carriers on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean join Delta Air Lines, which boasts 92 as of now, and JetBlue Airways with 65, to round out the top five.
  • Recent findings suggest that the A220 began as the CSeries before Airbus acquired a controlling stake in 2018.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Air France took delivery of its 60th Airbus A220-300 on November 6, closing out a five-year narrowbody renewal program. That milestone underscores the regional jet's growing global fleet and its place among the world's largest operators. Joining the French flag carrier on that podium are two airlines that exclusively fly the A220: Breeze Airways, with 57 and growing, and airBaltic's 55-strong fleet.

The budget carriers on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean join Delta Air Lines, which boasts 92 as of now, and JetBlue Airways with 65, to round out the top five. Notably, SWISS International Air Lines, which was the launch customer for the airframe, still owns just 30 aircraft. The jet's difficult development and launch after Airbus acquired the platform from Bombardier is just one part of the story.

Recent findings suggest that the A220 began as the CSeries before Airbus acquired a controlling stake in 2018. The Swiss order ended after it replaced its aging Avro RJ100 regional fleet, partly due to the ongoing engine crisis that has plagued the plane despite the otherwise popular airframe. Persistent durability issues and supply-chain bottlenecks with the Pratt & Whitney PW1500G engines forced operators worldwide to ground jets and even strip some for viable powerplants, keeping as many flying as possible.

Latvian flag carrier airBaltic introduced the stretched A220-300 in December 2016 and retired every turboprop and Boeing 737 by 2020 to run a pure single-type fleet. The most recent data places the carrier fifth globally with 55 aircraft listed on its roster, according to Airport Spotting. However, not all of those are airworthy. Groundings peaked at 13 parked jets in early 2025, wiping out thousands of seasonal flights across Europe and forcing costly replacement wet leases.

Industry observers note that restructuring aims shrink the active fleet from 54 jets to 36 by year-end and put 40 undelivered orders under review, even though the airframe itself never caused the crisis. Operated purely on its merits, the airframe exceeded expectations across both scheduled flying and wet lease contracts. Its low fuel burn let airBaltic restart routes profitably at lower passenger loads after the pandemic while leasing up to 13 aircraft to SWISS and Lufthansa Group partners.

Flying one 145-seat cabin simplified crew training, cut maintenance complexity, and supported flights stretching 3,450 nautical miles (6,389 km) from Riga to leisure markets like Tenerife. The vulnerability sat beneath the wing, where the A220 certifies only Pratt & Whitney's PW1500G geared turbofan.

When metal defects in turbine blades triggered urgent inspections and stretched engine overhauls past 200 days, airBaltic had no alternative supplier to fall back on. Engine availability recovered early this year, yet years of grounded aircraft left airBaltic financially fragile when unhedged fuel bills spiked following the recent conflict in Iran. On September 14, the carrier filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in Latest York, naming Pratt as its largest creditor.

Air France secured third place globally on November 6 when its 60th A220-300 arrived in Paris before opening service to Prague three days later, per Airline Geeks. That handover fulfilled the 2019 commitment to retire outdated Airbus A318 and A319 aircraft serving its network. Five years after entering service, the 148-seat fleet has carried nearly 24 million passengers and established the A220-300 as Air France's latest medium-haul mainstay.

Sources indicate that finishing the original batch roughly a year behind its initial 2025 target still left four 20-year-old A318s on the winter schedule. Industry-wide delivery delays and Pratt's PW1500G recalls tightened spare availability. As a result, Air France extended A318 operations to March 27, 2027. Rather than stopping at 60 jets, however, Paris now anticipates a 61st A220's arrival and is keeping 30 options plus 30 purchase rights.

Route economics and passenger demand are driving Air France-KLM Group leadership to envision growing toward 90 or 95 A220s. Its five-abreast cabin puts 80% of travelers in a window or aisle seat with 20% more overhead bin volume, while free high-speed WiFi already reaches 85% of the fleet, with full installation expected by February 2027.

JetBlue holds second place globally after counting 66 A220-300s in October out of its 100-aircraft total order, according to the Center for Aviation. That expansion completed the carrier's September 2025 phase-out of the Embraer E190. Trading 100-seat E190s for 140-seat A220-300s cut operating costs per seat by 29% and fuel burn per seat by 40%, projecting $4 million to $5 million in annual gains per jet.

Meanwhile, passengers benefit from bigger seats measuring 18.6 inches (47 centimeters) wide, the roomiest economy seating in JetBlue's fleet. That comes alongside 35 inches (89 centimeters) of pitch in extra-legroom rows and 32 inches (81 centimeters) in standard rows. The jets also have upgraded seatback screens and free high-speed WiFi.

According to recent reports, even at scale, JetBlue saw disruption from Pratt's engine recall as well as the Airbus factory bottlenecks in Mirabel and Mobile. Fiscal reports indicated the airline opened the year with four aircraft parked over PW1500G shortages. After engine removal, the planes spent roughly 200 days in overhaul shops. Supply-chain delays also forced Airbus to trim JetBlue's delivery schedule, pushing its final three firm aircraft into 2030 and beyond.

Sources indicate that eliminating the E190 still consolidated JetBlue into an exclusively Airbus operator, streamlining pilot and mechanic qualifications alongside its A320 and A321neo fleets. The transition also unlocked longer transcontinental routes for its smallest aircraft.

Breeze climbed to fourth worldwide when its final Embraer E190 revenue flight landed in Latest Orleans from Orlando on September 7, following acceptance of the 57th A220 in July, per Airport Spotting. This autumn deliveries pushed the Salt Lake City carrier over 60 jets out of 90 firm orders and 30 options for more. That fleet blueprint follows the design of Chief Executive David Neeleman when he ordered 60 jets in 2018, right after Airbus took over the program.

Neeleman revisited the decision in an Aerospace Global News story in September of this year, saying: "Our long-term strategy has always been to leverage the strengths and efficiencies of the Airbus A220-300 to help us cost-effectively scale our unique business model which centers around offering affordable, nonstop flights from unserved and underserved markets.".

In a recent development, breeze fits 137 seats inside the A220-300, pairing 125 economy chairs behind 12 Ascent first class recliners pitched at 39 inches (99 centimeters), flying 91 cities across more than 300 routes where 85% to 90% carry zero nonstop rivals. That 3,400 nautical miles (6,297 km) reach outclasses the Embraer E195-E2 and older Boeing 737-700s, opening cross-border flights to Cancun, Punta Cana, Montego Bay, Nassau, Costa Rica, and Santo Domingo.

According to recent reports, running one modern airframe slashes spare parts inventory and simplifies pilot scheduling compared with airlines splitting narrowbody flying across multiple cockpits. Meanwhile, the premium front cabin fills faster on thin leisure routes than any other regional jet could match. The airline has seen its 'long and thin' city pairs become steadily more profitable routes as a result.

Delta Air Lines has consistently led the global rankings by a wide margin, with 87 counted in July before third-quarter figures raised its roster to 92 jets, per Aviation Daily Report. Unlike the single-variant fleets run by JetBlue, Breeze, Air France, and airBaltic, Delta flies a split roster of 45 A220-100s averaging seven years old and 47 newer A220-300s with 145 firm orders.

It has been revealed that atlanta built its fleet on an order of 75 Bombardier CS100s from April 2016. That triggered Boeing's 2017 trade complaint, which was later linked to the proposed 292% US tariff. Chief Executive Ed Bastian held firm in October 2017, according to Reuters, saying, "We are not going to pay any tariff, and we do expect to take the airplanes," just before Bombardier transferred majority control to Airbus and set up final assembly in Mobile, Alabama.

US trade commissioners unanimously threw out those tariffs in January 2018, clearing Delta to launch A220 service from Upcoming York's LaGuardia. Today, it deploys two variants from coast to coast as 25-year-old Boeing 717-200s and even older A319s are phased out. Looking ahead, the gap between top operators will widen further as Airbus eyes a 2027 launch decision on a stretched Airbus A220-500. The new variant would seat 160 to 185 passengers, with deliveries targeting 13 jets per month from 2028.

At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
  • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
  • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

It has been revealed that “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

“I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews stated, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” remarked Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of Fresh York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

In a recent development, “I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

In a recent development, leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

It has been revealed that A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” noted California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

Industry observers note that #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, unveiled he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

Industry observers note that they’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” stated Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

Sources indicate that where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

In a recent development, battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

#INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun introduced his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

Upcoming leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint.     💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

    Sources indicate that he attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

    Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an revision, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

    The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

    This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

    Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:.

    Industry observers note that “The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the organization has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”.

    Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

    Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG.

    Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

    One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

    However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

    I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

    Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the blueprint is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

    Some fresh security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

    This resumption is a major deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

    Tech Report: Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027.
    • In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route introduced — it operated seasonally once weekly.
    • In a recent development, what’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

    In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route introduced — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

    In a recent development, what’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

    Industry observers note that the territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

    This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:.

    The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

    The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

    In a recent development, the route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:.

    Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM.

    The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

    It has been revealed that I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

    If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

    In a recent development, as you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

    In a recent development, air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was introduced in the first place, and is sticking around.

    In a recent development, while the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

    • Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a new project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”.

    • Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a new project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”.

    It has been revealed that playbill has since released an apology claiming it “incorrectly approved” the job posting for its site, and is now reviewing its internal processes. “We know this listing has upset and offended many, and the fact that it made it onto our site has disappointed those who trust us as an outlet. For that, we are sorry, and are committed to regaining your trust,” the statement reads. In response to the post, some people have demanded that Playbill take more accountability by explaining exactly how such a thing was approved for the site, expose who is behind the musical (though that was already public), hire more minorities to prevent similar wrongdoing in the future, and glitch apologies to the Floyd family and the black community. Others have more firmly called for barring the musical’s creative leader from the platform entirely.

    Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    On “A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?”.

    Industry News: Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase.
    • This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:.

    If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

    Recent findings suggest that the Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

    According to recent reports, rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

    Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who presently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

    It has been revealed that when it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being stated, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

    The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

    The card also has no extra cost to add authorized consumers, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

    Sources indicate that the Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    Sources indicate that you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    In a recent development, now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only upcoming rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

    The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:.

    According to recent reports, personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

    As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

    According to recent reports, rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    According to recent reports, starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    Sources indicate that one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

    In a recent development, southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

    Preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

    The Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

    According to recent reports, extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

    Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

    The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

    With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

    With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

    It has been revealed that southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

    In a recent development, on your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

    It has been revealed that in other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

    If you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

    The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

    Sources indicate that many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

    Sources indicate that that said, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

    First, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

    Industry observers note that the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

    Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:.

    The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

    There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:.

    I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

    It has been revealed that if you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:.

    Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

    Sources indicate that if you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

    If you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later.     How JetBlue's Bag Fee Hike Makes A BlueFirst Base Fare From $249, Bag Included, Look Like A Real Alternative

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, changes are happening at JetBlue Airways.
    • At the same time, JetBlue will soon introduce 'BlueFirst', a domestic first class cabin that will be rolled out fleetwide.
    • Industry observers note that jetBlue offers three fare types for its Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst, and Mint cabin classes: Base, Standard, and Flex.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, changes are happening at JetBlue Airways. The airline recently raised its bag fees for economy passengers; as of November 3, the first checked bag will cost between $50 and $70, depending on the day and when the ticket is booked, while a second checked bag ranges from $70 to $85. These are steep prices and noticeably higher than the checked bag fees set by US legacy carriers, while JetBlue's base fares before optional add-ons tend to be lower than the competition.

    At the same time, JetBlue will soon introduce 'BlueFirst', a domestic first class cabin that will be rolled out fleetwide. The carrier will debut this cabin on December 8 on its route from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, before introducing the cabin throughout its network. While JetBlue prices all fares dynamically, BlueFirst one-way fares will start at $249 when the cabin is first introduced, and while this certainly doesn't mean all tickets will be priced this way, those that are will be very compelling compared with the airline's economy cabin.

    Industry observers note that jetBlue offers three fare types for its Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst, and Mint cabin classes: Base, Standard, and Flex. None of the fares for Main and EvenMore include checked bags, meaning passengers who want to check their bags need to add at least $50 to the overall price of their tickets. At the same time, the airline's fresh BlueFirst fares do include at least one checked bag, while the BlueFirst Flex fare includes two checked bags. What makes this particularly notable is that BlueFirst fares are actually fairly attractive.

    In a recent development, the airline's one-way BlueFirst fares start at $299 from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, and the route between LaGuardia and Fort Lauderdale follows shortly afterward, with prices starting at $249. Although most tickets are being sold for significantly more, the airline has largely priced BlueFirst fares at about 40% to 70% more than an equivalent Main ticket.

    Crucially, however, even the BlueFirst Base ticket includes a checked bag, slightly closing the gap. The BlueFirst Flex includes two checked bags, whereas a Main Flex or an EvenMore Flex fare includes none. While the full cost of a BlueFirst ticket will still be higher, it's closer than expected.

    Industry observers note that with the recent increase in bag fees, BlueFirst tickets do look quite attractive for passengers who will check a bag and are willing to pay more for a better experience. BlueFirst offers a large recliner with added legroom, as well as complimentary meals and premium drinks. It undoubtedly offers a more comfortable experience than Main, and the price difference is not particularly steep once ancillaries are factored. What's more, JetBlue's initial pricing for BlueFirst does not follow the standard practice in the US.

    Sources indicate that generally, the US legacy carriers (which are the airlines that have offered domestic first class the longest) do not price first class tickets at 40% to 70% above economy. Domestic first class fares are usually significantly more expensive than economy tickets, and even when you factor in ancillaries, first class comes at a real price premium. Admittedly, JetBlue's initial BlueFirst tickets are being sold in the competitive Florida market, where fares tend to be low, but they still largely undercut the legacy carriers on price.

    One way to view this is as a deliberate strategy by JetBlue. The airline has never before offered a domestic first class cabin, and it plans to introduce BlueFirst throughout the network fairly rapidly. Not only do potential customers need to be made aware of the product and exposed to it, but the carrier also needs to pull customers away from American, Delta, and United. Attractive initial fares help with publicity while increasing bookings, which heightens awareness.

    In a recent development, on the flip side, however, airlines generally charge what they think is the maximum price that customers are willing to pay. JetBlue undercutting competitors on price can also be seen as a reflection of the carrier's pricing power, which isn't a positive sign. One reason JetBlue introduced BlueFirst was to increase revenue, since first class generally commands higher fares. If it continues to undercut competitors on price system-wide, then this would become a problem.

    It has been revealed that jetBlue operates like a budget airline, such as Frontier or Allegiant Air. However, the airline has differentiated itself not necessarily through low fares, but through the passenger experience. The carrier offered significantly more legroom in economy, along with seatback screens before they became common on domestic flights. In addition, snack options were diverse, and the airline's later Mint business class on transcontinental and transatlantic routes has been well received.

    According to recent reports, despite its low-cost carrier structure, the airline offers a passenger experience similar to that of legacy carriers, and arguably better in some ways. However, JetBlue has been unable to command a fare premium for its excellent economy product, while its Northeast operations come with high operating costs. In addition, the airline didn't offer first class in the past, further limiting revenue, and the carrier has faced serious challenges expanding its customer base.

    Boston Logan International Airport (BOS).

    Fort Lauderdale Hollywood International Airport (FLL).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    In a recent development, fresh York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

    Orlando International Airport (MCO).

    San Juan Luis Munoz Marin International Airport (SJU).

    According to recent reports, while JetBlue is an attractive option for customers in the Northeast, its route network is quite minimal outside of the East Coast. Its network and schedules are not attractive to much of the country. In addition, JetBlue has also suffered major reliability challenges. This hurts its appeal to many potential customers, as operational reliability is a major factor in purchasing decisions. While BlueFirst won't solve all of JetBlue's problems, it should help the carrier with its network-wide revenue problem.

    Industry observers note that not only do premium seats such as domestic first class have superior margins to economy seats, but premium demand is through the roof in the US. By not offering a domestic first-class product until now, JetBlue has essentially lost out on lucrative revenue, and several other low-cost carriers are now offering such a product. Frontier and Allegiant Air have both revealed domestic first class cabins to debut in 2027, while Breeze Airways already sells first class seats.

    Notably, JetBlue will largely maintain the same capacity its planes currently have. It will achieve this by cutting seat pitch in Main down to just 30 inches (76.2 centimeters), even though the airline has long been known for offering above-average seat pitch. While this is undoubtedly a drawback for most customers, JetBlue hasn't been able to command a fare premium for offering more legroom. Therefore, it will focus on where the money is, which is in the upcoming BlueFirst cabin, while it will also make its cabins more space-efficient.

    Of course, BlueFirst won't solve all of JetBlue's complications; the airline has limited national relevance, and on-time operations remain challenging. What's more, JetBlue's overall financial situation has deteriorated significantly over the past several years. However, the new BlueFirst cabin should help the airline's revenue stream and also make the airline more appealing to potential customers, who may have stayed away from the airline due to the lack of a domestic first class cabin.

    For travelers living in New York, Boston, Florida, or San Juan, JetBlue offers fairly comprehensive schedules and good route options. However, airlines such as Delta Air Lines and United Airlines operate routes that span the entire country, making them relevant nationally. In addition, these airlines have long offered domestic first class, which is a major reason to be loyal to one airline. What's more, JetBlue's operational reliability issues make customers more hesitant to choose it over other airlines.

    According to recent reports, the airline has not made money since 2019 and has posted a $257 million loss for the third quarter of 2026. The carrier has attractive assets, including a large slot portfolio at New York JFK Airport, and is generally liked by its loyal customers. However, the route network loses money, and frequent-flyer engagement is not high enough to offset these losses (legacy carriers make most of their money through co-branded credit card engagement rather than ticket sales).

    According to recent reports, the carrier has been implementing the 'JetForward' turnaround blueprint to cut unprofitable routes, improve operational reliability, and refocus on leisure customers. BlueFirst is one of the most consequential decisions the airline has made in recent years, and it should significantly improve the carrier's revenue stream given strong demand for premium cabins today. What remains to be seen is whether the JetForward initiative and moves such as introducing BlueFirst will be enough to ensure the airline's long-term survival.

    Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world.
    • Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.
    • Sources indicate that that said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

    Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

    Sources indicate that that said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

    Recent findings suggest that part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

    After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself….

    Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

    In a recent development, this is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

    Sources indicate that getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

    The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

    According to recent reports, however, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

    Industry observers note that ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

    Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

    Where do you stand on flying Ryanair?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1042 w)

    Latest FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.
    • As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports.
    • To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

    To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”.

    The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

    Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

    Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:.

    The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

    Recent findings suggest that I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

    Sources indicate that I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major problems, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

    If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

    I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a substantial difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot indicates “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy.

    Sources indicate that while the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉.

    As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

    I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

    In a recent development, bermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The organization has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

    Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

    For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

    As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

    Recent findings suggest that to my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

    Industry observers note that several months back, BermudAir revealed newly introduced winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

    In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:.

    On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with upcoming seasonal services in the following markets:.

    Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed….

    I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these upcoming markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:.

    Recent findings suggest that what’s interesting here is how the airline unveiled seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know….

    It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

    Sources indicate that bermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has revealed latest routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

    It has been revealed that I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”.
