    United Airlines Pilot Suspended On TSA Orders Over Support For Terror Group, Report Indicates

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has reportedly directed United Airlines to suspend a pilot last week over alleged support for a terrorist organization.
    • It has been revealed that the reported intervention follows several controversies surrounding United pilots and comes amid heightened international scrutiny of aviation personnel following an attempted terrorist attack aboard a flydubai flight in September.
    • The federal intervention reportedly occurred between November 16 and 22, and included the withdrawal of the pilot's Known Crewmember (KCM) credential, which facilitates expedited security screening for eligible airline employees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has reportedly directed United Airlines to suspend a pilot last week over alleged support for a terrorist organization. According to a report by Jewish News Syndicate (JNS), citing a federal government source, the pilot's crew security credential was also revoked. Neither the pilot's identity nor the terrorist organization they allegedly supported has been disclosed.

    It has been revealed that the reported intervention follows several controversies surrounding United pilots and comes amid heightened international scrutiny of aviation personnel following an attempted terrorist attack aboard a flydubai flight in September. CNN reports that US security agencies have subsequently issued a joint advisory to the aviation industry warning of renewed calls for attacks against commercial aviation.

    The federal intervention reportedly occurred between November 16 and 22, and included the withdrawal of the pilot's Known Crewmember (KCM) credential, which facilitates expedited security screening for eligible airline employees. The existing program is already undergoing significant changes, with the Association of Flight Attendants confirming that its replacement, the Crewmember Access Point (CMAP) program, will be administered directly by the TSA by the end of 2026.

    The suspension follows earlier reporting by journalist Mike Wagenheim on November 17, citing two sources who alleged that United was aware of up to six additional crew members who had expressed support for terrorist organizations. According to View From The Wing, the federal source subsequently alleged that resistance from the pilots' union contributed to the TSA's decision to intervene.

    Industry observers note that JNS approached both United and the TSA for comment on multiple occasions, but was not able to obtain a response from either organization. However, Michael Wilson, spokesperson for United's Master Executive Council of the Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA), explained that the union assesses allegations against its professional ethics code and United's workplace guidelines, stating that:.

    “[The union] has a robust professional standards committee and legal team that evaluates any accusation or pilot action.”.

    The latest case follows renewed scrutiny of United Captain Ibrahim Mossallam, a Newark-based pilot qualified to operate the Boeing 757 and 767. United initially suspended Mossallam with pay in November 2023 after he published social media comments praising the October 7 Hamas-led attacks on Israel. According to Airline Ratings, he subsequently returned to flying duties, although Aerotime reported last month that United had confirmed that he had again been removed from service pending a review.

    A separate controversy emerged in October when the Jerusalem Post reported that Israeli authorities had barred United pilot Sina Amjadian from operating flights into the country following allegations of support for Hezbollah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, United responded that that Amjadian, a Boeing 737 pilot, was not qualified on United's long-haul aircraft, and had been on leave since 2024.

    Mossallam publishes controversial comments concerning the October 7 attacks.

    United suspends Mossallam with pay.

    Mossallam reportedly returns to flying duties.

    Amjadian begins a leave of absence.

    United confirms Mossallam has again been withheld from service.

    United denies reports of Mossallam's immediate reinstatement.

    Israel's restrictions on Amjadian become public.

    Allegations emerge concerning six additional crew members.

    TSA reportedly orders the suspension of an unnamed pilot.

    Details of the reported TSA intervention are published.

    It has been revealed that while United has confirmed the employment status of both previously identified pilots, several other allegations remain unverified. The carrier has also explicitly denied reports that Mossallam returned to flying immediately after his latest suspension. Nevertheless, the reported intervention by federal authorities raises vital questions about where an airline's responsibility for assessing potential security threats ends, and the government's begins.

    The potential consequences of insider threats were demonstrated on September 30, when a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv became the subject of an attempted terrorist attack involving its first officer. The aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia, and the UAE's attorney general subsequently characterized the incident as an attempted suicide attack.

    In the US, the TSA's authority extends considerably beyond airport security checkpoints. Under Section 46111 of Title 49 of the US Code, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) must take action when notified by the TSA of a qualifying security threat. The TSA can also request that the action take immediate effect and, separately, issue mandatory security directives to airlines.

    Prevents flying for that employer.

    Withdrawal of crew security privileges.

    Removes expedited crew access privileges.

    Requires airlines to implement specified security measures.

    Temporarily removes relevant flying privileges.

    Removes privileges conferred by the certificate.

    Although there is no evidence that the United pilots were planning similar attacks, the broader security threat remains real. On November 19, the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and TSA jointly warned US airlines and airports about extremist calls for further attacks following the flydubai incident. While authorities were reportedly unaware of any specific credible plot, the advisory underscores the importance of preventative security measures, rigorous personnel vetting, and federal intervention powers.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1081 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    LATAM Refused My Refund Within 24 Hours, And The Reason Makes No Sense

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked.
    • Recent findings suggest that LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline.
    • This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked. I called customer service to cancel within the 24-hour cooling-off period, but was refused a refund for the most convoluted and unnecessary reason.

    Recent findings suggest that LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline. It’s an airline I look forward to flying with for several reasons. However, this recent booking experience has uncovered a gaping hole in its customer service, which in the air I’ve always found to be excellent.

    This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.

    The Brazilian site has no issue when entering UK credit card details.

    Recent findings suggest that however, the default setting for postcodes (ZIP codes) is numerical-only because, as in the US, Brazil’s postcodes consist only of numbers. In the UK, they’re made up of letters and numbers, so I couldn’t add the postcode that my credit card is registered to.

    In a recent development, I tried using only the numbers of my postcode (the one in the example above is random), but the site returned an error, saying it failed to connect to my bank. My guess would be this wouldn’t be a problem for US credit cards, given that ZIP codes consist only of numbers too.

    I remember this happening previously, but I never had an issue with a booking that I couldn’t change online.

    Ideally, I would have paid with a Brazilian bank account or credit card, but I’m still working through the immigration bureaucracy required to open one.

    It has been revealed that first of all, I tried to cancel by logging into my LATAM Pass account, but was redirected to the contact center. This is when I realized how much of an obstacle my booking via the UK website would be.

    After being put on hold 3 times for what seemed like forever, the agent I spoke with at LATAM’s Brazilian call center told me there was nothing she could do to help me.

    According to recent reports, she explained the only way I’d get a refund was to call the UK call center, since I’d paid in GBP on the UK website. I called just before the cut-off of the 24-hour cooling-off period, so by then I had exceeded it. I had only left it so close to the cooling-off period because I was researching the trip again the following day and found a better deal; otherwise, I wouldn’t have wanted to cancel.

    If I had called sooner and had more time, I could have asked someone in the UK to call for me, as my Brazilian phone number can’t make outgoing international calls. I did top up my UK SIM Card with 20 GBP, but at a charge of 2 GBP per minute, the call disconnected after 10 minutes on hold with no answer.

    Sources indicate that irrespective of whether I could have found an easier way to contact the UK call center, I can’t help but feel that my problem should have been resolved there and then over the phone by the Brazilian call center agent. After all, I booked directly through the airline’s website, and then called the airline directly to cancel. It makes no logical sense!

    Because of a stupidly convoluted system, I’m stuck with a LATAM ticket that I can no longer cancel, even though I called customer service within the 24-hour cooling-off period.

    It’s not the end of the world, as we can still take the flights we’d originally booked, but it’s so frustrating to be put in a situation like this in 2026 because of such an archaic technicality.

    I’m still a big fan of LATAM itself, and will continue to fly it, at least until my Platinum status runs out next year.

    What’s the most frustrating post-sale customer service experience you’ve had?

    Tech Report: House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    In a recent development, “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    In a recent development, “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

    When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    Industry observers note that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she remarked in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    Recent findings suggest that “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack said in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., stated everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he said at Thursday’s meeting.

    Orient Express Sailing Yachts Review: Corinthian’s Suites, Dining, Amenities, Service, And More

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 34 min read (6724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~34 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that orient Express Sailing Yachts voyages are best booked through Accor Preferred travel advisors.
    • For the main event of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, Ford and I had the chance to spend four nights on the Corinthian, which is the first ship in Orient Express’ newly introduced cruising venture, known as Orient Express Sailing Yachts.
    • It has been revealed that orient Express Sailing Yachts set sail in the summer of 2026, and with just 54 suites that can accommodate up to 110 guests, it really brings luxury cruising to a latest level.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that orient Express Sailing Yachts voyages are best booked through Accor Preferred travel advisors. They can get you the best price, and also add a shipboard credit. Ford and his team are happy to help with any requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

    For the main event of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, Ford and I had the chance to spend four nights on the Corinthian, which is the first ship in Orient Express’ newly introduced cruising venture, known as Orient Express Sailing Yachts.

    It has been revealed that orient Express Sailing Yachts set sail in the summer of 2026, and with just 54 suites that can accommodate up to 110 guests, it really brings luxury cruising to a latest level. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry more broadly, given how competition has been heating up.

    It has been revealed that I also recently reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, and had a great experience, and reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which is definitely more luxurious, but also has some growing pains. Lastly, I’ve compared all the experiences as well.

    Recent findings suggest that while Orient Express Sailing Yachts is the highest priced cruising venture to date, I have to say, the experience really is unbelievably good, and at least you feel like you’re getting an amazing experience. I come into these kinds of trips with a critical eye, and I was just blown away by the ship’s design, the quality of the food and drinks, and the service. To me the ship felt like a step back in time (in terms of its classic elegance), while also being cutting edge modern.

    In a recent development, if you can swing this experience, I’d highly recommend it. Okay, enough of an intro, here comes my 8,500-word review (yikes, this is the longest review I’ve ever published of anything).

    Orient Express Sailing Yachts charges per suite (rather than per person, based on double occupancy), and you’ll find that journeys typically cost an average of $4,000-6,000 per cabin per night for a base suite. Make no mistake, this is the very top end of the cruise market, and at this point you’re paying safari prices for the experience.

    It has been revealed that let me also emphasize that rates go up from there, and Orient Express Sailing Yachts has some of the most insane suites you’ll find at sea, some of which can cost six figures per sailing. Right now, Orient Express offers cruises in Europe in summer, and in the Caribbean in winter, with transatlantic sailings in the spring and fall.

    For what it’s worth, you’ll find rate parity regardless of which booking channel you reserve through. So your best bet is to book through a travel advisor affiliated with Accor Preferred, because they can add perks to your journey. The size of the credit depends on the accommodation type booked, plus the length of the journey. Ford and his team are of course happy to help with these bookings, and can be reached at [email protected].

    Recent findings suggest that in the interest of full disclosure, Ford was invited on this Orient Express Sailing Yachts journey (due to the amount of volume he books), and I tagged along with him. All opinions expressed are my own, and I strategy to review this exactly the same way I reviewed the two previous cruises (which we paid full price for). I haven’t been asked to write anything, and I have no incentive to be anything other than honest. If people are going to drop a ton of money on a luxury cruise, I want to make sure they’re at least getting the best experience possible.

    Recent findings suggest that we experienced Orient Express Sailing Yachts in early October 2026, shortly before the ship’s transatlantic sailing. Admittedly it wasn’t the most exciting itinerary, but that’s just what worked out for us in terms of timing, since we wanted to minimize our time away from home, had to schedule it around when family could best be with our kids, etc. Below is the itinerary for the sailing we took.

    We were happy with this itinerary, since our primary goal was to see the ship. It definitely wasn’t the most exciting, though, given that we docked at the port in Mahón (rather than tendering), and it also meant we didn’t have a marina day (not that you’d necessarily want that in October, since it’s a bit chillier). But the point is that if you’re traveling more in peak season, you can expect a marina day more consistently.

    Sources indicate that historically, cruising has been all about offering an all-inclusive experience. That’s true with Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, but then Four Seasons Yachts countered the trend, by only including breakfast, and then charging extra for lunch, dinner, and drinks (I don’t love this concept, especially given the quality problems they have).

    According to recent reports, while Orient Express Sailing Yachts might charge a lot, what I really appreciate is how the company has an ultra all-inclusive concept, to an extent that’s even greater than you’ll find on most other cruise lines. Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys include the following:.

    Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys don’t include the following:.

    Regarding the Orient Express Sailing Yachts tipping policy, the company states that gratuities are included in the fare — “however, if you wish to offer a tip as an extra gesture of appreciation, it will be warmly received.”.

    According to recent reports, I just have to emphasize that the level of inclusions really impressed me. Seriously, I was served caviar with breakfast, lunch, and dinner at various points (and even cocktails!), and the house champagne is Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 (which retails for around $200 per bottle).

    Orient Express Sailing Yachts right now has a single ship, which is named the Corinthian (a second ship is being introduced in 2027, and it’ll be named the Olympian).

    It has been revealed that the ship entered service in 2026, and is 722 feet (220 meters) long, 82 feet (25 meters) wide, and 26,600 gross tons. With 54 accommodations and a maximum capacity of around 110 guests, there’s a roughly 1.5:1 staff to guest ratio, given that there are around 170 staff onboard. The spaciousness of this ship, and the amount of space allocated to each passenger, really is next level.

    It has been revealed that the Corinthian also has the title of being the world’s largest sailing yacht, as it has three automated SolidSail rigid sails on tilting carbon masts, to provide wind propulsion, alongside hybrid LNG auxiliary power. It’s just such an elegant and distinctive looking ship, that it can’t help but turn heads. For those curious, it was explained that the sails reduce emissions by around 10%, and no, the ship doesn’t “heel” in the way a smaller sailboat would. Unless you’re looking up, you wouldn’t realize there are even sails.

    You can find the full Corinthian deck plan here. As you’d expect for a sail boat, there aren’t quite as many floors as on a traditional cruise ship. Guests can access a total of five floors, between levels three and seven. To briefly cover that:.

    Near the ship’s entrance, you’ll find a very cool directory of sorts, which reveals the floorplan of the ship. You can click any amenity, and then it will light up, so that’s super handy.

    According to recent reports, the ship has two sets of elevator banks, as well as two sets of staircases, so getting around the ship is really easy. We always used the stairs, since we were typically within a couple of floors of where we needed to be.

    As you’d expect, the ease of boarding a ship varies greatly depending on its size, but Orient Express Sailing Yachts really took it to the next level in terms of how seamless it was. We had spent a night at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. Our journey included the transfers, so an Orient Express representative met us at the hotel, and then we were driven to the port.

    According to recent reports, getting onboard the ship literally couldn’t have been easier. There were no formalities in the port, but instead, we were escorted straight through security, and then check-in was handled once onboard.

    There were no other guests as we boarded, and the staff really went above and beyond — for example, the crew member who escorted us through security and onto the ship insisted on holding an umbrella over our heads, to shade us from the sun.

    It has been revealed that our check-in process onboard took all of five minutes, and at that point we were introduced to our butler, Reuben, who escorted us to our suite, and took care of everything from there. I should mention how Reuben was German, so they specifically appointed us a German butler, which I thought was super fun (so we communicated with him exclusively in German).

    Industry observers note that we didn’t have a stop that involved tendering, but for those situations where you do, it’s an efficient process, given how few guests there are. Our one stop had us docked in port, and there was a nice seating area outside the ship with bottled water, sunscreen, etc. Admittedly a setup like this is more useful when you’re waiting on a tender, rather than just walking directly onto or off the ship.

    According to recent reports, orient Express Sailing Yachts has 54 suites onboard, spread across over a dozen different categories. The entry level suites here are among the most spacious at sea, while the penthouse suites really take luxury and space to the next level.

    Our sailing was rather empty — only 19 of the 54 suites were occupied — and we were upgraded to a higher suite category (I believe they had blocked most of the entry level room categories, as they were doing some minor updates to them ahead of the ship heading to the Caribbean). So let me share my thoughts on that suite first, and then I’ll share some pictures of other suites that I had the opportunity to tour as well.

    It has been revealed that we stayed in an Appartement Prestige, which is one of the more premium standard suite categories, but below the duplex suites and penthouse suites. These suites are marketed as being an average of 1,119 square feet (104 square meters), so they’re incredibly spacious.

    It has been revealed that we were assigned suite 518, located on the fifth floor. The hallways on the Corinthian are just stunning, as you can see below. It really feels more like a luxury hotel than a ship, especially in terms of the width of the hallway.

    The concept of forgetting that one is on a ship continued inside the suite. The interior felt more to me like a “Palace” hotel in France, than what you’d expect at sea. I can’t even imagine how much money was spent on the interiors, as the quality of the finishes, from the wall treatments to the carpet, as well as the furniture, was just unreal.

    Upon entering the suite, there was first a dining area with a table and a chair, as well as a desk with a chair (that chair could also be moved over to the dining table). It’s not often you get this kind of space in a cruise ship suite.

    In a recent development, the minibar was also in this area, and was well stocked, with everything being complimentary. This included a Nespresso coffee machine, cocktails, wine, beer, soft drinks, etc. They were also happy to replenish the minibar however you wanted, so there are really no limits.

    That entry area then flowed into the living room, which was gorgeous. It had a couch and a coffee table, as well as a hidden TV (which would pop up from in front of the mirror).

    Waiting on the dining table was a lovely welcome amenity, consisting of some freshly baked treats, a fruit plate, and a bottle of Veuve Clicquot 2015 Rose. There was also an Orient Express branded journal, along with two Orient Express water bottles, which guests could take home.

    Double doors then led into the bedroom, which had a very plush king size bed.

    Much like with the bedroom, the bathroom will make you forget that you’re on a ship, as it had double sinks, a soaking tub, a walk-in shower with amazing water pressure, and a toilet in a separate room.

    There were also a couple of closet areas, so there was plenty of space to store luggage and clothes.

    The suite then had a balcony that stretched the entire length of the suite, with very comfortable furniture.

    Beyond the generally beautiful design, it has to be pointed out just how over the top everything was. I mean, the deck furniture uses fabrics from Loro Piana, just to give you a sense of just how high-end it is.

    Housekeeping in the room was great (it was taken care of twice daily, and always well timed), butler service was very useful (more on that a bit later, when I talk about service), Starlink Wi-Fi was lightning fast, and I also love how Orient Express Sailing Yachts includes laundry. You could get unlimited washing, dry cleaning, etc., so that’s a very nice feature.

    Sources indicate that in the interest of checking out different suite products, I also had the chance to tour the Suite Panoramique, which is the entry level accommodation onboard, located on levels four and five. These are 506 square feet (47 square meters), so they’re spacious for an entry level suite on a cruise.

    This had the same general design concept as the suite we were in, except there wasn’t a fully separate living area. The suite had a comfortable king size bed, a desk with a chair, a dining table, and a huge window with a double daybed of sorts.

    While there was no bathtub, the bathroom still had double sinks, a walk-in shower, and a toilet in a separate room.

    To point out the obvious, these entry level suites don’t have balconies. Of course people prefer to have balconies, but this is just a simple reality of the difference between sailboats and cruise ships, in terms of how many levels there are, how far above water they are, etc.

    Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ top end suites are really next level, so I also had the chance to tour the Zephyr Suite, which is located on level seven, and is the second most premium suite onboard. This two bedroom suite has 2,486 square feet (231 square meters) of interior space, plus a terrace that’s 1,206 square feet (112 square meters).

    What I thought was so cool was how unique the design of this suite was, as the top suite products seem to have a totally original design. This very much had a residential vibe, with a long hallway connecting the various parts of the suite.

    Seriously, check out this living room….

    However, perhaps the coolest feature was the replica of an Orient Express Heritage cabin, intended to pay homage to the legendary train.

    The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has two pools onboard, with one being rather traditional, and one being unlike anything else at sea (at least to my knowledge). The main “leisure” pool is located on the fifth floor, at the back of the ship. While the pool has beautiful aesthetics and lovely deck space around it, this isn’t some destination pool in and of itself. So if a huge pool is a crucial factor in picking a ship, Four Seasons Yachts might be a better option.

    Industry observers note that we’re all different, and personally, I’m not much of a pool person. Quite to the contrary, I actually loved this pool deck, since it was mostly covered and in the shade, so I could nicely sit there and enjoy the breeze (funny enough, Four Seasons Yachts has an amazing pool, but I didn’t actually spend much time there, due to the lack of shade).

    The ship then has a second pool, which is among the most memorable you’ll find on any ship. The lap pool is 54 feet (16 meters) long, and it’s located under the sails. It really feels like you’re in a cave, since it’s on a deck that’s one level down from the main upper deck. What a pool!

    It has been revealed that on the pool front, really my only disappointment was the lack of a hot tub. As much as I find hot tubs to be kind of gross, I do love them, especially on a ship, so I was sad there wasn’t one of those. In general, the newer ultra high end cruise lines seem to be lacking in that department (the same was true on Four Seasons Yachts).

    Beyond the pool setup, on the seventh floor you’ll find a huge deck you can hang out on. There are lots of lounge chairs out here, though it’s not necessarily that popular for just lounging around. The star of the show here is what’s above.

    It has been revealed that the time when the deck really gets popular is when the ship pulls into or out of ports, given the panoramic views from up here, plus the ability to watch the sails be lowered and raised. I must say, it was absolutely mesmerizing to watch. They made a major event of departures, with live music, cocktails, etc. It really felt like a cocktail reception, only more intimate.

    Speaking of deck space, another fun aspect of the ship is how you can actually just freely walk up to the deck in front of the bridge, and even all the way to the bow. How fun!

    The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian wellness complex is located on the fourth floor, and that includes a Guerlain Spa. This area is an impressive 5,380 square feet (500 square meters), with four treatment suites (including a double suite), as well as all kinds of other traditional spa facilities.

    Guests can always use the facilities, even without an appointment, and that includes a sauna, steam room, relaxation area, locker rooms, etc.

    The spa treatment rooms are absolutely gorgeous, whether we’re talking about the couples room, or the individual ones.

    Ford and I got a couples massage during our final day (where we were at sea), and I can honestly say it was one of the best spa treatments I’ve ever had. Not only was the therapist I had incredible, but the massage bed was so comfortable, and there was something so calming about the view, the gentle sway of the ship, etc.

    For those curious about the pricing, you can find part of the spa menu below.

    According to recent reports, the ship also has a full hair salon and barber shop, so there are no shortage of opportunities to get your grooming needs taken care of here. The barber shop even leads to the speakeasy — more on that later.

    The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has a gym located on the fourth floor, which can be accessed by guests 24/7. The gym isn’t huge, but is more than sufficient given the size of the ship, in my opinion. Every time we used it, we were alone.

    The gym had a good selection of cardio and weight equipment, as well as a separate room for aerobics, boxing, etc.

    There was an excellent personal trainer onboard, and it was possible to schedule sessions with him at no extra cost. So it’s not just for group fitness, but even for personal sessions, on a space available basis. That’s really nice, as virtually any other cruise would charge for that, in my experience.

    Recent findings suggest that the Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has an incredibly impressive entertainment area, located on deck four. The issue is, it’s not really used a whole lot. Now, I’m not sure I’d actually call this an “issue,” but let me explain.

    When you think of mega cruise ships, nightly demonstrates and entertainment are among the most popular attractions. The thing is, the smaller the ship is, the less interest there is in things like this, and that’s especially true for the cruise lines that are primarily targeted at people who haven’t historically been cruisers.

    So the Corinthian has a huge theater with dozens of seats, but there’s not a whole lot that goes on there.

    Perhaps the more interesting entertainment feature is the private cinema, where you can have them screen a movie (or whatever) for you.

    There’s even a recording studio onboard — what a cool concept, and in addition to being able to play instruments here, I heard people have used this to record podcasts, etc.

    On the topic of entertainment, the ship also has a card room on the fourth floor, with chess, checkers, decks of cards, etc.

    Separately, there’s also the yacht club, which is basically a very elegant lounge area where guests can hang out, watch TV, etc.

    It has been revealed that lastly, the ship has the library on the fourth floor, which has an incredible selection of books. Everything on the Corinthian is so thoughtful, including the book selection. As it was explained to us, the 1,500-book library is supposed to represent the most vital books of the century, and were curated by the historic Parisian bookshop Galignani.

    I know there’s sometimes confusion about whether Orient Express Sailing Yachts is kids friendly, and the answer is… sort of.

    According to recent reports, on most voyages, guests onboard must be 16 years of age or older. However, on dedicated family voyages, children ages six months to 15 years old are allowed as well. Infants under six months aren’t permitted onboard, and per the terms, “families traveling with little ones under two years old must be accompanied by a dedicated babysitter throughout their voyage.”.

    Quite honestly, it’s logical that Orient Express Sailing Yachts would have this policy, since the ship’s venues feel really intimate, the pools aren’t huge, etc.

    In a recent development, for family voyages, the Corinthian does have a kids club onboard, which offers activities with a dedicated team. Babysitting services can also be arranged for excursions or gala evenings. But in terms of being kids friendly, I definitely think it’s an area where Four Seasons Yachts wins, as all voyages are kids friendly, the pool is huge, and there’s both a kids club and teens club.

    Orient Express Sailing Yachts has an incredibly impressive selection of restaurants, bars, and lounges onboard, with the culinary vision overseen by well-known chef Yannick Alléno. Before I get into details, let me just say that I found the quality of food and drinks onboard to be truly exceptional.

    I try not to exaggerate, because I think far too many people are a little too generous when describing food on cruises (or flights, for that matter — what’s with all these people describing airplane food as Michelin dining?). However, I found the quality of catering on Orient Express Sailing Yachts to just be in a completely different league than Four Seasons Yachts.

    Industry observers note that I was also delighted by the generosity of the included options, with an incredible alcohol selection, caviar accompanying dishes at breakfast, lunch, and dinner (and even cocktails), etc. It’s also interesting to note that no reservations are allowed onboard, except at the fine dining restaurant that costs extra.

    Everything was always available whenever we wanted it, though people will otherwise probably have mixed feelings on that policy (conversely, the concern when you do allow reservations is that people hog them and then just cancel at the last minute, leaving other guests with limited options).

    Anyway, here are the most significant outlets onboard Orient Express Sailing Yachts:.

    With that out of the way, let’s get into the venues in a bit more detail.

    According to recent reports, la Terrasse is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ all-day dining restaurant, serving breakfast, lunch, and dinner. It’s located at the back of the sixth floor, and has both indoor and outdoor seating. The fact that this is the casual restaurant really tells you the quality of the experience, as there are white tablecloths all hours of the day.

    This is the primary restaurant where breakfast is served, and you can find that menu below.

    Breakfast is entirely a la carte, though at the start of the meal, a basket with a rotating selection of croissants and pastries was brought out.

    There was a large selection of fresh juices and coffee available. My one disappointment was that the coffee was just okay, and clearly came from a machine. That’s ironic, because there’s plenty of delicious barista coffee on the ship, so this seems to be one of the only venues where that’s the case. Given the quality of service onboard, I’m sure they’d also be happy to get you a coffee from somewhere else, if you prefer.

    We found the breakfast selection to be very good, and over the course of our stay tried the acai bowl with coconut and seasonal fruit, chia pudding with fresh mango, the mixed berry plate, the crispy and soft blinis with caviar cream and smoked salmon, the avocado toast, and more.

    We also came to La Terrasse one day for lunch, and you can find that menu below.

    We split the chickpea hummus with parmesan to start, and then had the smoked salmon club sandwich and Thai beef salad as our mains. At our server’s insistence, we finished off with a floating island for dessert. YUM.

    We also had dinner here our first evening, and you can find that menu below.

    To start, we had the smoked salmon with blinis and sour cream, and the gazpacho.

    Then for mains, we had the pepper crusted beef fillet with cognac and cream sauce, and the red tuna teriyaki style, along with some sides.

    Lastly, we finished off the meal with a selection from the cheese trolley, plus the vanilla millefeuille.

    Across the board, the food and service were exceptional, so it’s amazing that this is just the most basic restaurant onboard, as it only gets better from there.

    L’Ecrin is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ elevated dinner restaurant, with a focus on seafood and pasta. It’s located on the sixth floor, and it exclusively has indoor seating. This restaurant doesn’t cost extra, but in my opinion is on par with the paid restaurant on some of the other top ships.

    We went here one evening for dinner, and you can find the menu below.

    At the start of the meal, we were offered some sinfully delicious bread, along with some cured meats. I’ll talk more about service in a bit, but I might as well just mention in passing how good the crew was about our dietary preferences. For example, we mentioned when we boarded how we don’t eat pork, so without having to say anything, we were brought something that fit our needs.

    Sources indicate that we took an unusual approach to ordering. To start, we shared the seabass carpaccio with citrus marinade, and the spaghetti with caviar. My gosh, not only was the caviar portion on the spaghetti massive, but the overall flavor of the dish was incredible, as the beurre blanc combined with caviar had quite the unique flavor profile.

    Then for mains, we had the warm lobster with olive oil and mayonnaise and the caponata and polenta. Again, this was very, very good.

    For dessert, while I had heard amazing things about the suzette pasta (flambeed tableside), we decided on the signature bronte pistachio ice cream coupe, which was insanely indulgent.

    It has been revealed that what a meal! This was definitely my favorite restaurant onboard.

    La Table by Yannick Alléno is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ most premium dinner restaurant, and it’s the only venue that comes at an extra charge, at the rate of €400 per person for the tasting menu.

    First, we have to talk about the restaurant as such. Can you believe this is on a ship? This is without a doubt the most beautiful dining venue I’ve ever seen on a ship. With just over half a dozen tables, it’s also a really intimate space.

    The tasting menu is constantly changing, and you can find the menu for our dinner below.

    I’ll let the pictures speak for themselves….

    The meal was very good, with service that matched the food quality. It really felt like a Michelin-starred dining experience in terms of the presentation, the service flow, etc.

    Sources indicate that while this was excellent, I will say, I wouldn’t necessarily feel compelled to dine here again. That’s just because the standard restaurants are so great that I don’t necessarily think it’s worth the incremental cost. At a minimum, don’t feel like you’re missing out if you don’t eat here… but definitely do take a look at the restaurant, to appreciate its beauty!

    L’Encre is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ venue that’s exclusively open for lunch, and it was definitely my favorite lunch spot onboard. It’s basically a circular counter with a little over a dozen seats, so the setting is stunning.

    You can find the menu below. Think of the concept as basically being like a seafood omakase, where they just keep bringing you out more dishes. Of course you can customize however you want, ask for more of whatever you really like, skip dishes, etc. Below is a sampling of what we ate.

    Sources indicate that la Piscine Lounge is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ poolside venue, serving drinks, snacks, and even full meals, throughout most of the day. It’s even opening at night, and can double as a bar for a pre-dinner drink. It’s a beautiful space, definitely not your typical pool bar!

    You can find the drink list and menu for that below.

    We had an afternoon snack here one day, and split the mezze and the veggie burger, both of which were very good.

    Le Bar de la Bibliotheque is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ coffee shop in the library area, and it’s a lovely place from which to get some work done, read a book, etc.

    Here you’ll find barista coffee, homemade cakes, fresh juices, kombucha, and more.

    Le Wagon Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ primary bar venue, and it’s only open late at night. It’s intended to be a replica of the circular bar found on the modern Orient Express trains, with 1920s and 1930s heritage craftsmanship, so it’s a very cool space.

    There’s a DJ there at night. The one thing to be aware of is that it only opens really late (9:30PM at the earliest, but often 10PM), and if you’re on a quieter sailing, there might not be too much of a vibe here. However, I’ve heard that on other sailings this place can be packed — it’s all about the crowd on a particular cruise.

    You can find the drink list below.

    I ordered the signature Corinthian Martini, with gin, vodka, champagne cordial, and — naturally, like everything on this ship — caviar!

    Next, Le Speakeasy Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ speakeasy. The idea is basically that people do a bar crawl, and it’s common to move between both bars in the same evening. Much like Le Wagon Bar, this one also opens really late.

    The bar is located through a hidden door in the barbershop, so they’re really committed to that speakeasy theme.

    This bar even has a separate smoking room, which I’m sure smokers will appreciate (as it’s the only indoor space on the ship where you can smoke).

    This bar also has some unique signature cocktails, and you can find that drink list below.

    While not included, they are very proud of their liquor selection here, with some bottles that are older than my dad (and at a cost of up to $2,400 per shot — yowzers!).

    In a recent development, tempted as I was, I stuck to one of the included martinis. 😉.

    Le Flybridge Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ outdoor bar space located on the top floor. While this is open quite frequently, it really only gets busy when the ship sets sail, given the interest in watching the sails in action.

    According to recent reports, orient Express Sailing Yachts of course has 24/7 room service, which is included, with no additional costs. The standard room service menu is on the basic side, but service very much falls into the category of them wanting to make guests happy, so they’re also happy to get you something from any restaurant, if you’d like (but since the menus are always changing, they’re not published in the room service menu).

    We did have room service dinner one evening….

    …and the final morning we had breakfast in our suite as well (we accidentally ordered too much).

    Our amazing butler, Reuben, also gladly brought us cappuccinos and protein shakes, so they were happy to accommodate guests however they could.

    In a recent development, orient Express Sailing Yachts has a very impressive included drink menu. You can find the standard alcoholic drink list below, though some venues have additional options or signature cocktails customized to that venue.

    Industry observers note that having Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 as the house champagne is very impressive. And let me just say, they’re also not cheap with the pours — you can barely go anywhere without having a glass pushed on you. 😉.

    Of course there’s also a premium drink list with even more special wines and spirits, and those come at an extra cost.

    In a recent development, I have to acknowledge that our sailing was rather empty, so the staff to guest ratio on this sailing was unreal. That being said, it wasn’t just the ratio that was amazing, but the quality of staff was really incredible as well. If you don’t have good staff, they’ll find a way to disappoint even if the staff to guest ratio is amazing.

    I’m not exaggerating when I say that service on Orient Express Sailing Yachts was flawless in terms of attention to detail, and that was such a contrast to our Four Seasons Yachts experience.

    It has been revealed that it’s hard to even pinpoint any one area that impressed me, because it was just very consistent, polished, and proactive, across the board. Let me just give a few examples:.

    As I said in my Four Seasons Yachts review, while we had an amazing time, we had way more service issues than I’d consider to be acceptable, given the price point. This was exactly the opposite, and it was just flawless service experience after flawless service experience. So while I’m sure service is consistently good, I’m sure the empty sailing also contributed to taking this to the next level.

    We were definitely on an odd sailing, in terms of seasonality, since we were on the second to last voyage before the ship sailed across the Atlantic, to start the winter season in the Caribbean.

    According to recent reports, our sailing was empty, with just 19 of the 54 suites occupied, so there were fewer than 40 guests. It really felt like having a private yacht, as we rarely saw others, and we’d go to restaurants for dinner, at most a handful of other tables would be occupied.

    It has been revealed that on our sailing, almost everyone seemed to be a European retiree, so it was maybe in line with what you’d expect from the stereotypical guest profile of Orient Express trains. However, Ford has had some clients on Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and based on the feedback he has gotten, the ship can be an absolute scene, with some pretty over-the-top people.

    The guest profile that Orient Express Sailing Yachts gets is probably a bit different than almost any other cruise line. For one, the ship has already been chartered multiple times in its first season, so you can imagine the kinds of people we’re talking about. And even on sailings that haven’t been chartered, there have been some A-list people onboard.

    So anyway, we had a very pleasant, understated crowd onboard, but I’ve also heard the crowd can make for quite some people watching, especially for sailings in the South of France, etc.

    As I said at the beginning, my goal here is to be as objective as possible, so what feedback do I have? Honestly, as much as I have a critical eye, I think there are shockingly few areas for improvements. Here are the things that stood out to me:.

    According to recent reports, I also want to acknowledge that Trek Trendy had published a review of the Orient Express Corinthian, and I think that’s worth watching for a different perspective. I think he was being totally fair with some of his critique, but I had a different experience:.

    I travel a ton, and as much as I have so many amazing experiences, I’m almost always excited to go home, given that I miss family, and travel is sort of my “job.” I have to be honest, the Orient Express Corinthian was the first time in recent memory where I thought to myself “man, I wish it weren’t over.”.

    Sources indicate that earlier this year I experienced Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection and Four Seasons Yachts, and they’re both great in their own ways. However, Orient Express Sailing Yachts is really in a different league. Yes, it’s priced at the top end of the market, but it also includes the most, and I really appreciate that. There’s something nice about paying a high voyage cost in advance, but then feeling like everything is included.

    Orient Express Sailing Yachts really is an unbelievable product, from the design of the ship, to the incredible restaurant and bar concepts, to the service. If you can swing it — and especially if you’ve never taken a cruise before — I can’t recommend this enough.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the next membership year, and it’s good news (well, at least for those who don’t requalify for their current status tier).

    Marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the 2027 status year, for situations where someone doesn’t qualify for a particular elite tier based on their activity in 2026. Specifically, elite members who don’t achieve the published criteria to maintain their status will only drop down at most one elite tier.

    In other words, Ambassador Elites will at most drop to Titanium Elite, Titanium Elites will at most drop to Platinum Elite, Platinum Elites will at most drop to Gold Elite, and Gold Elites will drop at most to Silver Elite.

    For what it’s worth, this policy matches Marriott’s historical approach to status soft landings. Before Marriott and Starwood merged, back when Marriott’s loyalty program was named Marriott Rewards, Marriott consistently had a status soft landing policy. With this, Marriott Rewards members never dropped more than one elite tier per year, regardless of their activity.

    Sources indicate that that policy has continued since the new program was formed, including for the next year. However, there’s no guarantee this will continue to be the policy in the future. For those curious, the status offered as part of the soft landing also does count toward lifetime elite status. So if you’re downgraded from Titanium to Platinum based on a soft landing, that year of Platinum will add to your total.

    According to recent reports, during the pandemic, we saw airline and hotel loyalty programs largely extend elite status several times. This made sense, given the extent to which business travel decreased for many. However, with the huge increase in leisure travel and all the fresh ways to earn elite status, we’ve seen elite ranks swell.

    Personally I think the concept of a status soft landing makes a lot of sense. After all, sometimes life conditions change for people, and in many cases those changes are just temporary. If you drop from top tier status to no status, you don’t really have much of an incentive to stay loyal to that hotel group when your travel picks up again.

    Industry observers note that by offering a soft landing, loyalty programs can try to build more of a long term relationship with members, and that’s a positive. We also see some programs allow members to pause their status for a year or extend status as a one-time exception based on life circumstances, and I think that’s a great policy as well.

    Marriott Bonvoy has a generous status soft landing policy for 2027, for those who don’t requalify for status in 2026. If you didn’t requalify for your current status tier with Marriott Bonvoy in 2026, you can expect that you’ll be downgraded at most one status level.

    What do you make of Marriott Bonvoy’s soft landing policy for status?

    Why A Part 103 Ultralight Needs No Pilot's License In The US & Weighs Under 254 Pounds

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology.
    • In a recent development, he at the moment holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair.
    • A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

    In a recent development, he at the moment holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

    A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

    Many people assume that flying any type of aircraft requires extensive training, a pilot certificate, medical approval, and federal registration. While that holds true for most types of licenses, such as a Certified Flight Instructor certificate (CFI) or Airline Transport Pilot (ATP), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has long maintained a narrow exception that allows certain recreational flyers to take to the skies without obtaining a pilot license. The exception falls under FAA Part 103, a section of federal regulations governing ultralight vehicles and the strict limitations placed upon them.

    Sources indicate that while Part 103 is broadly described as allowing someone to fly without a license, the reality is more nuanced. The regulation applies only to a highly specific category of lightweight recreational aircraft that must meet strict performance, weight, and operating requirements. Understanding what qualifies under Part 103 helps explain where the FAA draws the line between recreational freedom and traditional pilot certification requirements.

    Yes, you can legally fly an aircraft in the United States without a pilot certificate, but only if the aircraft qualifies as an ultralight vehicle under FAA Part 103. These vehicles occupy a unique regulatory category that exempts operators from requirements including pilot licensing, aircraft registration, airworthiness certification, and medical certification. The exemption was created to support recreational flying while limiting risk through strict aircraft performance restrictions.

    According to recent reports, for powered ultralights, the FAA limits empty weight to 254 lb (115.2 kg), fuel capacity to five gallons (18.9 liters), maximum level-flight speed to 55 knots, and maximum power-off stall speed to 24 knots. Because these aircraft are intentionally small and limited in capability, the FAA regulates them differently than conventional airplanes.

    Sources indicate that the concept dates back decades, when regulators sought a framework that would allow simple recreational flying without imposing the full regulatory burden associated with general aviation aircraft. Rather than focusing on pilot certification, Part 103 controls risk by limiting what the aircraft can do. According to the FAA's regulations, qualifying ultralight vehicles are intended solely for sport and recreational purposes and are limited to carrying a single occupant.

    Sources indicate that A common misconception is that any small aircraft can be flown without a license. In reality, FAA Part 103 sets detailed technical requirements an aircraft must meet to qualify as an ultralight vehicle. The term Ultralight is a specific category issued by the FAA for licensing and certification, such as airplane, rotorcraft, or glider for pilot ratings. While an FAA certificate typically prints the category and class, the lack of a true license requirement omits this display.

    In a recent development, the most notable requirements involve weight, occupancy, fuel capacity, and performance. Powered Ultralights operate on the basis of minimal configurations of these variables. Ultralight aircraft should not be confused with Light Sport Aircraft, the next category up in the FAA's classification; they also have slightly different regulatory requirements, such as a higher speed limit of 250 knots and the ability to carry an additional passenger. These privileges come at the cost of training for a sport pilot certificate, among other requirements as outlined in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart J, and 14 CFR Part 91.327.

    Maximum 5 gallons (18.9 liters).

    Industry observers note that unpowered ultralights, such as many hang gliders, fall under a different weight limit. Under Part 103, these vehicles must weigh less than 155 pounds (70.3 kg) empty. By restricting both weight and performance, the FAA effectively prevents Part 103 aircraft from evolving into conventional airplanes that would normally require certification and pilot qualification.

    Although operators are exempt from licensing requirements, they are not exempt from federal aviation regulations. FAA Part 103 establishes operational limitations designed to protect both ultralight pilots and the public on the ground. Interestingly enough, Ultralight aircraft are not governed by either 14 CFR Part 61 or Part 91, which is the usual home for general aviation operation guidelines.

    Sources indicate that among the most notable restrictions are where and when ultralights may fly. Operations are generally limited to daylight hours and must avoid congested areas, cities, towns, and open-air assemblies of people. The rules also restrict operations within controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, E, and most special use airspace) unless prior authorization has been obtained from air traffic control.

    Industry observers note that these requirements show that the FAA's approach is not deregulation but targeted regulation. Operators may not need a pilot certificate, but they are still responsible for understanding airspace, weather conditions, and applicable operating restrictions before every flight. For many ultralight enthusiasts, voluntary training remains a common safety practice despite the absence of a licensing requirement.

    In a recent development, while FAA regulations do not require formal flight training for Part 103 operations, aviation organizations consistently encourage it. Groups such as the Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA) have long promoted structured training programs for ultralight pilots, emphasizing that regulatory exemptions do not eliminate the risks associated with flight.

    Industry observers note that the EAA's Ultralight Sourcebook notes that Part 103 provides significant operational freedom but also places responsibility squarely on the operator. Similarly, many flight instructors and aviation educators recommend dual instruction in two-seat trainers before attempting solo ultralight operations. Pilot Institute has also highlighted that, despite the absence of licensing requirements, knowledge of weather, aerodynamics, and operating limitations remains critical for safe flight. Industry recommendations reflect a broader understanding that flying skills and regulatory requirements are not necessarily the same thing. A pilot may legally operate a Part 103 vehicle without a certificate, but aviation organizations generally view training as one of the most effective safety measures available.

    It has been revealed that cost is another notable variable. While flight training for a Private Pilot License (PPL) can range from $9,000 to $130,000, Ultralight aircraft operation has a less burdensome barrier to entry. Because no official license is required by the FAA, training costs alone are significantly lower. In general, however, ultralight aircraft are much less common in the general aviation landscape than, for instance, a Cessna 172. The good news is that outright ownership of ultralight aircraft is also more accessible. Aerocorner reports that the cheapest fresh ultralight aircraft in 2026 is the Mini-Max 1103R, a single-seat wood-and-fabric kit that Mini-Max USA lists at $10,899.99 for the airframe. Also available is a finished, ready-to-fly example at about $22,500.

    Industry observers note that the same restrictions that make Part 103 accessible can also limit its practicality. Ultralight aircraft operation is the strictest modality of aviation under the FAA's jurisdiction. While the qualifications are generally among the most accessible to the public, that accessibility comes with significant compromises. Aircraft designed to remain under the FAA's weight and performance limits generally offer less range, lower speed, and reduced capability compared to certified airplanes.

    Weather sensitivity is another consideration. Because ultralights are lightweight and often have minimal protection from the elements, operating conditions that might be manageable for larger aircraft can present greater challenges. The single-seat requirement also prevents pilots from carrying passengers or instructors during normal operations. Under Part 103, ultralight vehicles must fly during daytime hours with visual reference to the surface and meet basic Visual Flight Rules (VFR) weather minimums for their prescribed airspace. Reference to published manufacturer minimums is also imperative, particularly with respect to wind.

    Prospective ultralight pilots should also remember that local airspace considerations still matter. Before operating any Part 103 vehicle, operators should ensure they understand applicable airspace restrictions and any authorization requirements that may apply near busy airports. In the United States, ultralight aircraft cannot fly over congested areas or crowds, and they cannot enter controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, or surface Class E) without prior Air Traffic Control (ATC) authorization. Advisory Circular AC-91-36D also suggests that ultralight pilots voluntarily remain above 2000 feet (609.6 meters) above ground level (AGL) wherever possible.

    Recent findings suggest that the short answer is yes: FAA Part 103 allows certain ultralight vehicles to be flown legally in the United States without a pilot certificate, aircraft registration, medical certification, or airworthiness approval. However, that freedom exists only because the FAA imposes strict restrictions on aircraft weight, speed, fuel capacity, occupancy, and operating conditions.

    Rather than creating a loophole in aviation regulation, Part 103 represents a carefully structured compromise. The FAA permits recreational flyers to avoid many traditional certification requirements while ensuring that the aircraft themselves remain limited in capability and risk exposure.

    For aviation enthusiasts, Part 103 continues to provide one of the most accessible entry points into personal flight. Yet the regulation's enduring message remains clear: while a license may not be required, safe operation still depends on knowledge, preparation, and respect for the limitations of both the aircraft and the environment in which it flies.
