    #146774. Why Flight Attendants Sit Facing Backward During Takeoff & Landing

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1503 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Flight Attendants Sit Facing Backward During Takeoff & Landing

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Have you ever noticed that flight attendants sit facing backward during take-off and landing?
    • According to recent reports, the jumpseat is a very key part of an aircraft's safety equipment and is designed to protect the crew members during taxiing, takeoff, and landing, which are critical phases of flight when accidents are more likely to occur.
    • Industry observers note that flight attendants face backward in their jump seats during takeoff and landing primarily for safety.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have you ever noticed that flight attendants sit facing backward during take-off and landing? While most passenger seats are forward-facing, some business-class configurations have rearward-facing seats, which some passengers dislike; therefore, backward-facing seats are rarely used for passengers.

    According to recent reports, the jumpseat is a very key part of an aircraft's safety equipment and is designed to protect the crew members during taxiing, takeoff, and landing, which are critical phases of flight when accidents are more likely to occur. It is important that the crew are protected at these times so that they can evacuate the aircraft if necessary.

    Industry observers note that flight attendants face backward in their jump seats during takeoff and landing primarily for safety. During a sudden stop or impact, a rear-facing seat backrest absorbs the force across the back, shoulders, and head instead of concentrating it on a strap across the chest, as in a car. The seatback supports the head, neck, and torso during sudden forward deceleration, reducing strain on the spine and neck and improving force distribution.

    Rearward-facing seats are safer for the upper torso and reduce the impact on the body in landings or emergencies. Crew seats facing backward are designed to allow brace positions during normal or abnormal takeoff and landing and help protect against debris. That is why infants are encouraged to stay in backward-facing car seats for as long as possible. During sudden deceleration, your body naturally wants to keep moving forward.

    The jumpseat protects the crew from severe injury and helps them stay conscious and mobile in an accident, so that they can direct an evacuation and assist passengers in an emergency. They are always positioned near the emergency exits so that they can respond rapidly. In the event of an accident, cabin crew are better protected than passengers in forward-facing seats. The crew member needs to be conscious and uninjured in an emergency for a fast, efficient evacuation and to potentially save lives.

    It has been revealed that cabin crew jumpseats are almost always facing rearwards. While most face backward toward the tail, some jumpseats face forward or sideways depending on the aircraft type, cabin layout, and door position. They can be single or double jumpseats. Double jumpseats are usually found in the aircraft galleys at the main doors, while single jumpseats are often next to emergency exits throughout the cabin. On private jets, jumpseats are commonly forward- or side-facing depending on type, although they differ from those on commercial jets and may have a different harness and no safety equipment underneath.

    It has been revealed that forward- or sideways-facing seats still meet certification rules and use multipoint harnesses and brace positions to protect the crew. The seat base flips up when the crew member stands, so it doesn’t block the exit during an evacuation. The seats are heavily padded around the back and head area and are next to or inside the galley and adjacent to exit doors. A four-point safety harness secures the crew member firmly during take-off and landing. The lap belt must sit low and tight across the pelvis (not the stomach), with shoulder straps snug and free of twists. It has a single release point.

    Sources indicate that below each standard crew jumpseat, there is a container that holds the life vest, a torch, and a manual release tool for the oxygen system. An interphone is attached to every seat or double seat for communication with the crew and flight deck. Around the seat and above the seat, there will be a smoke hood, fire gloves, and a fire extinguisher. During the emergency equipment check, crew must ensure the harness is fully functional and fitted correctly.

    In a recent development, facing into the cabin allows crew members to observe the passengers and spot hazards during critical phases of flight. It also ensures passengers follow safety instructions and are seated when the seat belt sign is on. They can typically be used only by airline crew, depending on the airline's policy. There are more jumpseats than the minimum working crew onboard. There are also jumpseats in the flight deck, but there are very strict rules on who can use them.

    Sources indicate that these seats are strategically located so that the flight attendants have visibility over different areas of the cabin on take-off, landing and whilst taxiing. There is also the potential to spot unruly passengers or if someone is sick and needs help. They also need to prepare for the silent review in case of evacuation and observe outside conditions through the windows to prepare as needed.

    However, in the rear or aft galley, this would not be the case as the passengers cannot be seen clearly if the cabin crew are in their harnesses. On some aircraft types, such as the Airbus A320, one cabin crew seat in the aft is stored flat but maneuvered to face forward, and an extra crew member can observe the rear cabin from there if carried.

    While rear-facing seats offer strong impact protection, airlines generally keep passenger seats forward-facing due to passenger preference, motion sickness concerns, and structural or weight factors. Aircraft burn more fuel due to heavy rear-facing seats, making them less popular with airlines.

    According to recent reports, there is also some psychology behind them. Passengers don’t want someone facing opposite them as a rule, as it makes them feel uncomfortable. Some people don't like the sensation of flying backwards, and it could cause motion sickness in some people. It could also be an issue in an evacuation knowing which way to go, as passengers tend to head in the same direction as the door where they entered the aircraft.

    It has been revealed that although backward-facing seats are more commonly found in military aircraft, some airlines offer seats that face backward. If you do want to try out a rear-facing airplane seat, opt for business class seats with airlines like American Airlines, United Airlines, Qatar Airways, and British Airways. The brace position for passengers in rearward-facing seats is different from that of the standard brace position.

    According to recent reports, the cabin crew brace position is specifically designed to prevent the body flailing, protect limbs needed for opening emergency exits, and minimize head and neck injuries during an impact. When facing the back of the aircraft, impact forces push the body backward into the seat. The back and head should be firmly against the seatback and headrest to prevent whiplash. Knees are together, and feet are placed flat forward or back depending on the airline and whether facing forward or rearward.

    Hands should be placed under the thighs with palms facing up or down, depending on airline procedures, or may be placed on the knees and elbows tucked in to avoid fractures. If facing forward, the chin should be placed down towards the chest and feet slightly forward. In an abnormal landing, the brace position is the same apart from placing hands one on top of the other behind the head with elbows brought together in front of the face and not covering ears, so commands can still be heard. This may differ at different airlines.

    Where there is a side-facing jumpseat, feet should be flat on the floor, hands should be tucked under thighs or placed on the knees. However, extra support is needed, and the head and body should lean against the adjacent bulkhead or headrest on the side toward the direction of impact, securing the shoulder harness tightly.

    Industry observers note that crew adopt a "semi-brace" or standard brace posture during every normal takeoff and landing. This is often paired with a "silent review" of emergency exit procedures, so they are protected against sudden runway excursions or aborted takeoffs and prepared for any incident or accident. They secure themselves in their jumpseats on the flight crew's command: "Cabin crew seats for take-off" or "Cabin crew seats for landing.".

    Recent findings suggest that on most narrowbody aircraft, both the forward double jumpseat and rear double jumpseat face rearward, apart from the Airbus A320, which has another seat at the rear that faces forward into the cabin. On widebody aircraft, seats can be single at some exits, and the double seats in the rear galley may face forward depending on aircraft type.

    Industry observers note that in the United States, 14 CFR 25.785(h) says a flight attendant seat must be “near a required floor-level emergency exit”, that one must sit adjacent to each Type A or Type B exit, and that the rest must be “evenly distributed among the required floor-level emergency exits to the extent feasible”. The rule requires a flight attendant seat to be forward- or rearward-facing with an energy-absorbing rest supporting the arms, shoulders, head and spine, and to sit near a floor-level emergency exit. The brace position differs depending on which way the seat faces and the airline's safety procedures.

    Breaking: Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency.
    • Sources indicate that in this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically.
    • For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it.

    Sources indicate that in this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry.

    For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports.

    The exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome.

    According to recent reports, you do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening).

    Over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through.

    Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc.

    Recent findings suggest that global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032.

    If you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday.

    It has been revealed that generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from [email protected].

    You can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership at the moment expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early.

    According to recent reports, you won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire.

    Industry observers note that there is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time.

    If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period.

    In a recent development, it costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry.

    Recent findings suggest that when you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends:.

    Recent findings suggest that while only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process.

    On November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years.

    Note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a upcoming Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned).

    Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period.

    There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry.

    Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information.

    This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more.

    You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years).

    The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to update your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler.

    At some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few).

    To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay.

    When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one.

    I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days.

    As mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal. The email came from [email protected] with the subject line “TTP Application Status Change.”.

    Sources indicate that experiences seem to be mixed as to whether an interview is required for renewals. For example, during my last renewal, I did need to get an interview, while during my renewal before that, I didn’t need to get an interview.

    It has been revealed that the good news is that if you do need to be interviewed, you can typically just do so when you return from an international trip. When I did it, it took less than a minute.

    I just went through the process of renewing Global Entry, and it was pretty easy. You basically just have to confirm that all the information during your last application is still accurate, add all the countries you’ve been to since then, and pay a fee.

    In a recent development, this time around, the application was processed in 10 days, and there was a full approval, so no interview was required. However, don’t be surprised if you do need an interview, as that happened to me during my last renewal.

    Hopefully this is useful for anyone else who has a Global Entry renewal coming up soon.

    If you’ve had to renew your Global Entry, what was your experience like?

    It has been revealed that membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

    GAO chief nominee triggers partisan clash at Senate hearing

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday.
    • Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.
    • “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

    “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

    According to recent reports, democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also said Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

    Ueland said if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”.

    At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

    Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

    Recent findings suggest that “It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”.

    In a recent development, democrats remarked Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

    Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

    Sources indicate that democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

    Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

    Ueland did not give a direct response.

    “First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he remarked. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

    He also said it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”.

    Peters remarked when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

    “We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters said. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”.

    “That’s not so,” Ueland replied.

    Ueland said his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

    Ueland remarked he would give it a “medium grade over time.”.

    For example, he mentioned GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”.

    By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”.

    Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

    Ueland mentioned he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”.

    Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland said, “To be clear, yes.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, mentioned he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

    Industry observers note that paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

    And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

    In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

    “We see that bipartisan process as extremely crucial to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” mentioned Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

    Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, mentioned by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”.

    In a recent development, he mentioned GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”.

    The union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

    Industry observers note that however, as I’ll explain below, the reason you get the card isn’t just because of the welcome offer, but also because of the long term value that it offers. There are lots of great uses of Amex Membership Rewards points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air Canada Aeroplan, to Air France-KLM Flying Club, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give some examples of how points could be redeemed:.

    In a recent development, in line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus isn’t available to those who right now have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a few additional things to note:.

    Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to generally be among the easiest to get approved for. I also want to emphasize that Amex business cards not counting toward the 5/24 limit really makes the opportunity cost of picking up this card pretty low, for those of us into maximizing our rewards.

    The first thing to love about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is that it has no annual fee (Rates & Fees)… you can’t beat that!

    According to recent reports, but really what makes this card unrivaled within the Amex ecosystem is its return on spending, up to a certain limit. Specifically, the Amex Blue Business Plus offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year, and then 1x points. It’s that straightforward. So $50,000 in spending per year would earn you 100,000 Membership Rewards points.

    Industry observers note that this is the only no annual fee credit card on the market that earns 2x transferable points that can be moved to the full list of airline and hotel partners at the “premium” ratio. There’s literally not another card like that. The one caveat is that the card does have foreign transaction fees, so I wouldn’t recommend using it for purchases abroad (Rates & Fees).

    Speaking of the ability to move points to partners, I think that gets at the other thing that’s awesome about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card — in the event that you want to close other Amex cards (with annual fees) that accrue Membership Rewards points, this is a great card to have, so that you can maintain your points balance, given the ability to pool points.

    In a recent development, so I view this as a very low risk card to apply for, especially with it not counting toward Chase’s 5/24 limit. The only reason I wouldn’t get this card is if I’m otherwise at the Amex five credit card limit.

    Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Plus Card here.

    It has been revealed that in the Blue Business portfolio, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is the standout card for me. However, I should also mention the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which is essentially the cash back equivalent:.

    Industry observers note that personally, I get more excited by the Amex Blue Business Plus Card than the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, simply because I value Amex points at well over one cent each. That’s why I’d rather earn 2x points rather than 2% cash back. Admittedly, not everyone will feel the same, especially those who don’t actually want to put the effort into maximizing points.

    According to recent reports, the Amex Blue Business Cash bonus is also greatly improved, though, as it was previously for a $250 statement credit. So this is twice as good.

    Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Cash Card here.

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is a product that often flies under the radar. Ordinarily the card doesn’t have a very exciting bonus, but at the moment, we’re seeing a much better opportunity than usual. The card has a welcome offer as high as 50,000 bonus Membership Rewards points. Getting a no annual fee card that earns 2x transferable points (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1x points) that can be moved directly to airline and hotel partners at the most favorable ratio is something you won’t find on any other card. That’s why this card is in my wallet, and the welcome offer is just the icing on the cake.

    In a recent development, meanwhile if you’re looking for the cash back equivalent, it’s at least worth mentioning the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which has a bonus as high as $500 cash back as a statement credit. That no annual fee card earns 2% cash back (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1% cash back), also with no annual fee.

    These are both really lucrative cards that can be worth holding onto in the long run, so if you’re eligible, I’d absolutely recommend applying.

    Tech Report: Long-haul budget airline Norse Atlantic suspends flights

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (430 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Norway-based long-haul budget airline stated in a statement early Thursday that all flights were suspended "pending clarification as to whether a viable financing solution can be established.".
    • "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found," Norse added.
    • The confirmation followed the cancellation of all Norse flights late on Wednesday, the flight tracking website FlightRadar24 reveals.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Norse Atlantic Airways may be no more.

    The Norway-based long-haul budget airline stated in a statement early Thursday that all flights were suspended "pending clarification as to whether a viable financing solution can be established.".

    "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found," Norse added.

    The confirmation followed the cancellation of all Norse flights late on Wednesday, the flight tracking website FlightRadar24 reveals.

    Pakistan International Airlines, which contracts Norse to operate select flights, mentioned Wednesday evening on X that Norse had suspended operations "without prior notice.".

    In a recent development, norse flew just one U.S. route at the time of its shut down: Orlando International Airport (MCO) to London's Gatwick Airport (LGW), schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show.

    During the prime summer months, Norse also seasonally flew from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Athens International Airport (ATH) in Greece, LGW and Rome's Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

    It has been revealed that at its peak in 2024, Norse served five U.S. destinations, including Las Vegas's Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), from gateways in Europe.

    The collapse of Norse comes at a challenging time for airlines. Jet fuel is at historic highs, spiking after Iran war and other conflicts. Geopolitical tensions have closed significant swaths of airspace, including Russia and significant portions of the Middle East. And, high interest rates have pushed the cost of capital for any business to the highest levels in years.

    Norse warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical" and mentioned its continued operation was "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs.".

    Luis Gallego, the CEO of International Airlines Group that owns British Airways and Iberia, told the Financial Times in October that smaller airlines would struggle this winter due to the those financial headwinds.

    Norse was one of the last airlines trying to make long-haul, low-cost work between the U.S. and Europe. Play Airlines, which attempted the same strategy via a connecting hub at Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF), shut down in September 2025. And both Norse and Play were formed following the retrenchment and collapse of previous attempts; Norse from Norwegian Air's withdrawal from the market in 2021 and Play from the ashes of WOW Air that shut down in 2019.

    Only independent French Bee and the budget arms of the larger European airline groups, including Discover, Level and Edelweiss Air, continue to offer lower-cost transatlantic flights.

    Story updated with Norse confirmation of its shut down.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

    In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

    Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

    To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

    Sources indicate that the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:.

    The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:.

    If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

    The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

    If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

    Sources indicate that the annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

    It has been revealed that the math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

    With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

    Recent findings suggest that so my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a significant spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

    Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

    That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

    #146766. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2001 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).
    • Industry observers note that I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product.
    • Recent findings suggest that admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

    Industry observers note that I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

    Recent findings suggest that admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge challenges. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

    According to recent reports, ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

    Industry observers note that royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:.

    10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM.

    Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

    We arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

    Industry observers note that I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

    Boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

    We boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

    It has been revealed that royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

    These seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

    Recent findings suggest that the tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

    There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

    On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

    There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

    Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

    In a recent development, while the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

    Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

    So the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an issue. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

    During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

    One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

    Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

    At 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

    The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

    It was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

    The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

    After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

    Sources indicate that A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

    Recent findings suggest that the crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

    For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

    Just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

    There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

    Sources indicate that the lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

    Industry observers note that the primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

    At 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

    The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

    We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

    From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

    On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

    As we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

    It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

    Industry observers note that I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

    It has been revealed that to be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

    What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

    Unless the FO is going to reach over and steer the plane with the only tiller, I am sure the cap was steering the plane on the ground. I believe the 737 even the max only has 1 tiller.

    • Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept.
    • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
    • It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

    It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

    The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

    Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

    However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

    The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

    It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines.

    It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

    Industry observers note that democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately noted they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

    The "major four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

    "This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito said before passage.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

    Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

    The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

    That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

    The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

    The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

    None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

    Recent findings suggest that the bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, initiative and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

    The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

    The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

    Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

    Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as at the moment drafted.

    However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an concern: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

    And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the new Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

    Sources indicate that merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

    Recent findings suggest that some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

    "I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley remarked before the vote Thursday night.

    But Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental concerns under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

    While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

    As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

    However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

    In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

    Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

    Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

    Sources indicate that after decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

    Lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

    Latest Update: Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the spirit of trying out fresh ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.
    • Recent findings suggest that I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could.
    • After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the spirit of trying out fresh ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

    After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉.

    Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

    On this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That mentioned, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is right now undergoing some refurbishments.

    Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

    Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

    According to recent reports, speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall L. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge new flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

    I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

    Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

    If you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding….

    It has been revealed that thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

    Industry observers note that the legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My plan was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

    Of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

    I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

    No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

    In a recent development, of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

    Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

    I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

    Industry observers note that I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

    According to recent reports, for those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

    I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

    According to recent reports, despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical issue, so I didn’t take any pictures.

    I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

    Sources indicate that I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

    Industry observers note that neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

    In a recent development, air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

    I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

    The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

    I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

    As for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no problem.

    Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

    One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting fresh people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

    If I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

    Over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

    After being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

    Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

    When was the last time you flew long-haul in economy, and how was the experience?

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, there’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

    It has been revealed that so that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

    Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.

    I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir.

    In a recent development, I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w.

    According to recent reports, I can totally appreciate how frustrating it is when a flight is canceled, but this is actually very simple — federal regulations dictate the maximum number of hours that pilots can fly, and that’s for good reason. The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

    I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”.

    I’d like to point out what makes this even worse — this was a flight out of Miami last night, and the airport had shut down due to a ground stop, because a FedEx MD-11 ran off the runway. That was an absolute pain for all passengers out of the airport, and I can assure you that American also wasn’t happy about that happening, and the impact it had on its operations.

    All would be forgiven if this traveler either just didn’t say anything further, or acknowledged “ah, I wasn’t aware of that.” Instead, he has had dozens and dozens of posts, just going on and on and on.

    He posted about how American claimed the cancelation was the airport’s fault, but insisted “it’s actually these pilots fault,” and suggested “pilots will lie to save money for their firm.”.

    Industry observers note that @AmericanAir will cancel your flight the day before Thanksgiving and say it's the airports fault. It's actually these pilots fault. pic.twitter.com/v4t8KPSojR.

    @AmericanAir pilots will lie to save money for their firm @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/7VmOKILwCL.

    He then attacked American’s rebooking lines at Miami Airport. Look, I’ll be the first to call out American when they fall short (and they often do!), but if you really can’t figure out why rebooking lines “wrap around the corner” on one of the busiest travel days of the year when there was an accident that shut down an airport, then you really aren’t trying very hard to understand things.

    Recent findings suggest that @AmericanAir why do your rebooking lines always wrap around the corner? How bad are your operations? pic.twitter.com/Id8AaTiom1.

    He also has an issue with bathrooms at Miami Airport, which I get, but goodness, he’s repetitive.

    Why do you have the most disgusting bathrooms @iflymia.

    Why are your bathroom so nasty @iflymia.

    Why are your bathroom never clean@iflymia.

    Why are your bathrooms such a health hazard @iflymia.

    You should hire people to clean your bathrooms@iflymia.

    He then suggested that he’ll fly Delta or United next time, because they can get you where you’re supposed to go. Yeah, sure bro, they’ll get you out of Miami Airport when it’s closed due to an accident.

    Next time I'll fly @united or @Delta because they can actually get you where you are supposed to be when you are supposed to be there…and paid for…unlike the incompetent airline @AmericanAir. I bet your life is full of incompetence.

    He’s also asking Secretary Duffy to investigate American, because “they are the most unethical and corrupt firm in America.” We know the Trump administration loves to investigate corruption, I’m sure they’ll get right on that!

    Can you investigate @AmericanAir they are the most unethical and corrupt firm in America.

    It has been revealed that honestly, I think American is perfectly justified in banning this guy. He’s violating the firm’s policy on photographing employees, and this kind of behavior doesn’t need to be tolerated.

    Industry observers note that it sucks when things go wrong while flying, especially for travel around the holidays. But there’s a fine line between a reasonable complaint, and one that’s completely uncalled for.
