International first class had already been abandoned by Delta, United, KLM, Air Fresh Zealand, and Latam, on the view that improved business class delivers better returns for the space 9.

    The real tension is financial, not strategic. American cut its 2026 outlook twice and now expects a full-year loss of $1 to $1.60 per share, with Q3 revenue up 19.3% to $16.3 billion wiped out by a $1.9 billion fuel increase 5. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion 4. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate the returns that fund further improvements and pay down debt 3.

    Eliminating first class is how American funds business class scale — the question is whether a carrier losing money this year can out-invest Delta and United for the same premium travelers.

    The industry is moving the same direction. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft, while reducing first class from 14 suites to 12 6. Virgin Atlantic is replacing its onboard bars with more premium seats 2. Skift Research puts premium cabin revenue at $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 6.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    According to recent reports, tilting schedules toward high-yield local traffic in Fresh York, Los Angeles, and Chicago is a margin repair, not a differentiator. Those are exactly the markets Delta and United defend hardest, and American is attacking them with the weaker balance sheet. The local-market tilt only differentiates if it is paired with the reliability and premium product American has promised but not yet delivered fleetwide. 12.

    Recent findings suggest that chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that American is tailoring schedules toward higher-yield local markets in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago, while leaning on alliance partners to extend global reach 1. Local traffic — passengers starting or ending a trip in the hub city — pays more than connecting traffic, so the mix shift lifts unit revenue without adding seats. That matters now because fuel, not demand, is the problem: third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion while fuel expense rose 67.5%, leaving a $269 million net loss 4.

    Sources indicate that the local-market tilt is a yield lever American controls, which is why it is being pulled. The uncertainty is whether it can hold corporate and premium local share in three cities where it is the number two or number three carrier, while slowing growth to protect 2027 profitability.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    New York is where the gap between the substantial three is clearest, and Skift’s reporting shows three different postures rather than three comparable expansion programs.

    It has been revealed that american’s disclosed JFK looks are schedule and product additions, not a terminal program. Summer 2027 brings JFK–Nice and more Heathrow flying alongside new Philadelphia and Charlotte transatlantic routes.

    Delta co-financed its own Terminal 4 expansion with the Port Authority’s broader $18.9 billion JFK overhaul, giving it fixed infrastructure control at the airport.

    According to recent reports, united has no JFK slot portfolio of its own. The Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue, cleared by the DOT in July 2025, gives it borrowed access from Terminal 6, plus a net-neutral swap of eight Newark timings.

    American’s JFK position sits inside a broader catch-up effort. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion, and is on track to lose money in 2026 1. Its Upcoming York investment is showing up in aircraft and cabins — the A321XLR with 20 Flagship Suites, the 777-300ER with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seating — rather than in gates 21.

    According to recent reports, delta’s advantage is structural. Its Terminal 4 expansion let it consolidate all JFK flying in one facility, within an $18.9 billion airport redevelopment that also produced the new Terminal 1 and Terminal 6 34.

    United’s return is the newest variable. Seven daily round trips is small, but it ends an absence at JFK and comes without United buying slots 5. United’s CFO stated this week that the Blue Sky relationship stops short of a deal, pointing to JetBlue’s nearly $10 billion debt load 6.

    Industry observers note that skift’s coverage does not include a disclosed long-term American gate or terminal program at JFK comparable to Delta’s Terminal 4 investment. Treat American’s JFK plan as route and product-level on the current record.

    This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

    Shares are gross cash from bank partners, not profit.

    In a recent development, allegiant CEO Greg Anderson put the number on the record himself: co-branded credit cards are about 5% of Allegiant’s revenue, against roughly 15% at the legacy carriers and above that at Alaska and Southwest 1. He called closing that gap the airline’s biggest revenue catalyst, with more detail promised at an investor day 1.

    Apply that 5% to Allegiant’s actual revenue base and you get the realistic dollar figure. The firm posted $962 million in revenue in the quarter ended July 2026 and $943 million in the prior quarter, a run rate near $3.7 billion including Sun Country, which Allegiant bought for $1.5 billion and closed in May 1. That implies roughly $175 million to $190 million a year in card remuneration. The program had 600,000 cardholders and first-quarter remuneration up 9% 1. For context, Allegiant’s chief marketing officer said the Bank of America deal brought in $100 million in 2022, just over 4% of $2.3 billion in revenue 2.

    The structural reason leisure carriers sit at 4% to 6% rather than 15% is spend frequency. Sun Country’s then-CMO estimated a typical customer flies once every 12 to 18 months, which is why discounters pitch the card as a way to stay relevant between trips 8.

    Treat 5% to 7% of total revenue as the realistic planning band for a primarily-leisure U.S. carrier, and 10% to 15% as the legacy ceiling Allegiant is aiming at rather than a near-term forecast. Also note these are gross cash from banks, not margin — United’s Scott Kirby argues analysts count the payments and ignore the cost of carrying award passengers, and no carrier discloses that cost 3.

    This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

    It has been revealed that points stop being a moat once an agent can price them. What holds a member is what an algorithm can’t compare: recognition at the property or gate, reliable operations, and redemption the member can actually get. Skift Research found loyalty affiliation ranked last as a reason to trust an AI recommendation, while 83% of U.S. travelers say better personalization would make them switch programs. 21.

    The pressure is already measurable. Skift Research found 44% of U.S. travelers book outside their preferred program because prices are cheaper elsewhere, and 55% would follow an AI tool to a better deal 1. Among business travelers, consistently good service outranks rewards as a reason to return, 46% to 15%, and 62% say they are likely to switch for a better price or experience 3. Card programs have also taken the top of the rankings: 32% of travelers named credit cards and banks the most rewarding loyalty programs, ahead of hotels at 26% and airlines at 20% 4.

    The open question is whether recognition and service can be made legible to an agent. Google’s agentic hotel booking passes along only name, payment, occupancy, and property, keeping the conversation that produced the booking — which leaves the differentiators that matter most invisible at the moment of choice. AI referrals still sit below 2% at Booking and Marriott, per Bernstein, so the terms are being set while volume is small.

    This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

    For airlines, yes — so far. Card-spend status converts bank payments into the industry’s highest-margin revenue: Delta took $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, and co-brand operating margins run 35–50%. For travelers, the trade is worse: status is more crowded and benefits thinner. And the whole model rests on uncapped U.S. interchange fees that Congress could change. 23.

    The shift is now structural, not experimental. Delta made Medallion Qualifying Dollars the sole status metric from 2024, earned through flying, co-brand card spend, and bookings 5. American collapsed everything into Loyalty Points earned by flying, card use, or partner purchases, and told Skift the pandemic revealed loyal members who had never flown with the airline 6. Southwest is the latest: from January 1, 2027, cardholders earn one tier qualifying point per dollar spent under fresh silver, gold, and platinum tiers, with lounges built alongside Chase 4.

    The profitability of spend-based status is asserted more often than it is proven. United CEO Scott Kirby argues analysts count the cash banks pay for miles and ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers: “Nobody counts the cost.” Skift’s review of filings found United does not publish total cash received from banks, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 6.1 million in 2019 to 10.9 million in 2025, or 10.3% of passenger miles.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    No cut has happened, and none is imminent. The Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January 2026 after a Trump endorsement but still has not had a floor vote, and the $38 billion Visa/Mastercard settlement compresses standard rates while leaving premium tiers — the ones funding travel rewards — largely untouched. The risk to travel’s co-brand economics is Congress, not the courts, and the industry is betting Congress never acts. 1.

    In a recent development, U.S. interchange — the merchant-paid fee on each card swipe — remains uncapped, unlike in the EU, UK, and Australia 1. That single condition underwrites travel’s most profitable business line. Delta collected $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, American took $6.2 billion from co-brand and other partners, and Morgan Stanley estimates co-brand operating margins at 35-50%. 12.

    Sources indicate that where caps landed, rewards shrank. The EU and UK capped credit interchange at 0.3% in 2015, and no European airline collects anything close to $8 billion from a card partner 1. Australia’s Reserve Bank cut its cap to 0.3%, effective October 2026 and stated explicitly it was setting the level so issuers could no longer use interchange to fund rewards 1. The U.S. has run its own version: the Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange in 2011 and debit rewards largely disappeared 1.

    According to recent reports, the lobbying tells you what’s at stake. Airlines for America runs a “Protect Our Points” campaign, and the card and banking industry has spent roughly $200 million opposing swipe-fee reform 1.

    In a recent development, nothing in the current reporting points to a cut in the near term — the bill has been reintroduced three times without a vote, and the settlement spares the premium tiers. But the downside modeling the industry works from doesn’t contemplate reform at all: Morgan Stanley’s three paths for the travel co-brand market by 2035 ($100B, $60B, $40B) all assume the fee structure stays intact.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    In a recent development, neeleman’s current playbook is the opposite of the airline JetBlue became. At Breeze he avoids the Major Four entirely, flies thin routes no one else serves, and judges flying by trip cost rather than cost per seat. JetBlue today is losing money in exactly the overlapping markets he says he would never fly, and only now shifting toward Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, and cheaper terminals. 15.

    Industry observers note that this is a counterfactual, so treat what follows as analysis, not reporting: no one has reported what Neeleman would do at JetBlue. What can be grounded is the strategy he runs now and the position JetBlue is in.

    In a recent development, neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum this month that small U.S. airlines fail when they fly head-to-head with United, American, Delta, and Southwest, and that he “would never run an airline that’s overlapping those guys” 13. He pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it landed in the majors’ markets, and the majors added seats that cost them less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1. He remarked chasing CASM “got Spirit to die,” and that Breeze looks at trip costs instead, generating 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1.

    In a recent development, jetBlue, meanwhile, posted a $257 million third-quarter net loss on $2.8 billion of revenue, cut its 2026 margin guidance to negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, and watched bonds backed by its TrueBlue program trade at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 4. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and the bond market” and reaffirmed operating profitability in 2027 5.

    Industry observers note that the parts of JetBlue’s current initiative that most resemble Neeleman’s thinking — smaller-market growth out of Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, cheaper terminals including Spirit’s former LaGuardia slots — are the parts arriving last. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, and fuel at $4.64 a gallon in the fourth quarter is the squeeze in the meantime.

    One caution on the counterfactual: Neeleman’s founder-era JetBlue was a single-fleet, point-to-point, cost-advantaged carrier in a market that no longer exists. His own argument now is that the majors have gotten “so much better at what they do,” with credit card revenue, international networks, and loyalty programs a new entrant cannot attack directly 3. A Neeleman-run JetBlue in 2026 would face the same math every other mid-size U.S. carrier does.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    It has been revealed that the delivery crunch Skift has reported runs through the A320neo and 737 Max lines, where meaningful narrowbody slots are scarce until roughly 2033. Breeze doesn’t order from either. It flies the 137-seat A220-300, a separate Airbus program with far more room, and had about 44 firm A220s on order as of late 2025 with roughly 15 due in 2026. That gives Breeze growth capacity most U.S. carriers can’t buy right now. 13.

    The squeeze is real but line-specific. Skift’s Farnborough coverage put meaningful A320neo and 737 Max positions out of reach until about 2033, with widebodies tight into the mid-2030s, and lessors — not airlines — placing the biggest orders to absorb that risk 1. Skift Aviation Forum framed manufacturers as one of five counterparties now deciding which airlines absorb the fuel shock, with the same roughly-2033 horizon 2.

    In a recent development, breeze’s queue position sits on a different program. Cirium data cited by Airline Weekly in December 2025 demonstrated 44 operational A220s, six grounded for geared turbofan engine inspections, and 44 more on firm order, with David Neeleman saying about 15 would arrive in 2026 3. The A220 backlog has grown since — AirAsia’s 150-aircraft, $19 billion order in May 2026 pushed the program past 1,000 total orders and made it the largest single firm order for the type 4. That tightens the line over time, but Breeze’s positions were already contracted.

    Breeze can keep adding thin, exclusive routes while A320neo and 737 Max operators wait.

    Neeleman remarked Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM and generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic.

    Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan inspections have taken A220s out of service, which can cost Breeze more utilization than a slot queue would.

    The commercial read matters more than the queue. Neeleman told Skift Aviation Forum in November 2026 that Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, that it avoids the Big Four’s markets, and that it is pushing premium seating from about 41% to 45% of the cabin 5. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 5. He also pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the carrier that moved to bigger aircraft and landed in the majors’ markets 5.

    In a recent development, scarce A320neo and 737 Max slots cap industry capacity through roughly 2033, which keeps fares firm — and Breeze gets that pricing benefit without being stuck in the same queue, because it buys from a different Airbus line. The constraint on its growth is engine availability and demand in thin markets, not a place in the order book.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Neeleman manages to trip cost, not CASM, and flies A220s and E190s on routes the Substantial Four skip.

    Operating margin of 0.1% excluding aircraft sale-leaseback gains; adding first class and Starlink.

    Neeleman said majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat.

    The practical case for Breeze is that it usually isn’t a choice between carriers. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, and Neeleman said the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1. The alternative on most of those city pairs is a connection on a major or a drive.

    Recent findings suggest that the second difference is product. Breeze is a low-cost carrier that sells extra legroom, first-class-style seating, and free Wi-Fi, and it’s pushing premium seating from about 41% of total seats to 45% 17. That premium lean is now industry-wide — premium cabins generated 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion 4 — but Breeze built it in from the start rather than retrofitting late, as Frontier and JetBlue are doing now 58.

    In a recent development, reliability on thin routes is the third. Breeze flies dedicated aircraft carrying maintenance crews and spare parts, which Neeleman noted helps prevent cancellations on routes with few frequencies 2. On a once- or twice-weekly route, a cancellation can mean days, not hours.

    In a recent development, breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results, so the four consecutive profitable quarters are the tech giant’s own disclosure 1. Low frequency cuts both ways — fewer flights means fewer rebooking options. And Breeze has no interline agreements of the kind that would get you onto another carrier if things go wrong, which is the structural cost of a network built on routes nobody else flies.

    Industry observers note that breeze’s advantage is route selection, not price. The reason to pick it is that it flies nonstop where the majors connect you — and it has stayed out of the head-to-head fights that killed Spirit and are keeping Frontier’s margins near zero.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Recent findings suggest that low likelihood over the next few years. Breeze’s profitability rests on being the only airline on nearly 90% of its routes, and Neeleman has mentioned directly he would never run an airline overlapping the Major Four. Big-city flying would put Breeze against carriers whose seat costs are less than half what Spirit paid — the dynamic he blames for Spirit’s death. Expect large metros as spokes, not battlegrounds. 13.

    Breeze already touches large airports — Fort Lauderdale is one, where it expanded alongside JetBlue, Frontier, and Allegiant after Spirit’s May shutdown 6. The distinction that matters is whether Breeze flies into big cities on routes the majors also serve. On that, the strategy points the other way: 83% of third-quarter routes were exclusive to Breeze in late 2025 3, and Skift Research found it was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 1.

    The key uncertainty is what the IPO does to the growth story. Neeleman pushed a likely listing to 2027, and public-market investors tend to reward scale and recognizable markets. If Breeze needs a bigger growth narrative to price a deal, large metros are the obvious place to find one — and the place its cost structure is least suited to.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Sources indicate that breeze keeps trip cost low by flying a small, efficient airplane on routes nobody else serves, then filling it with premium seats and bundles so the flight clears its cost at low frequency. The durable part is the aircraft and the monopoly network. The fragile part is labor and fuel, which rise with age and scale — and the fix Neeleman is reaching for is more revenue per trip, not a lower cost base. 12.

    Recent findings suggest that neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum that Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — cost per available seat mile — and stated chasing the per-seat metric “got Spirit to die” 1. The logic: a smaller jet costs less to operate per departure, so a thin market can support it even when the seat-mile math looks worse than a major’s 2. Spirit’s error, in his telling, was upgauging into the majors’ markets, where the majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1.

    It has been revealed that breeze’s real defense is revenue, not cost. Premium seating is moving from about 41% of the total toward 45%, and Neeleman prepares a Priceline-style model starting next year that takes a commission on the real estate and spending its new routes create in small markets. Both raise revenue per trip rather than lower cost per trip — the admission that a startup cannot out-cost the Significant Four.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    American can be a premium player at 200M+ passengers, but not a premium leader on Delta’s terms. Its premium mix already works — about 30% of seats generate roughly 50% of revenue, and Q3 premium revenue rose 22.9%. The constraint is that a mostly domestic, Sun Belt-weighted network of that size dilutes yield faster than cabin retrofits lift it. American earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion. 321.

    Scale is not disqualifying by itself. American’s premium revenue grew faster than main cabin last quarter, 22.9% against 19.5% 2. The glitch is what the rest of the airline costs. Revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion in the third quarter while operating costs rose 19.7%, leaving a 1% operating margin against Delta’s 9% and United’s 7% 6.

    The catch-up list is real and expensive: Starlink on every mainline jet from 2027, seatback screens returning, A321XLR Europe routes in summer 2027, 777-300ERs with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seats, and Citi as sole co-brand card issuer 13. At least 50 revealed changes since early 2025 1.

    Sources indicate that the unresolved question is whether premium spending generates enough cash to fund the next round. American’s CCO Nat Pieper said consistent service, network, and loyalty revenue have to produce returns that pay for further improvements and reduce debt — and that reliability is the precondition. Skift’s reporting does not yet show those returns at scale. 45.

    Network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty all have to be working in concert.

    — Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines, at Skift Aviation Forum 5.

    This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

    Allegiant, now merged with Sun Country, serves 42 markets from Fort Lauderdale but only marginally targets former Spirit routes — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City. It is instead adding unique markets no one else flies, expanding the airport’s destination menu.

    JetBlue is Fort Lauderdale’s largest carrier and treats it as the third leg of a stool with Upcoming York and Boston, adding Mint transcons, domestic first class, and a possible lounge.

    According to recent reports, the short answer: Allegiant mostly doesn’t compete with JetBlue at FLL head-to-head. It competes around it.

    According to recent reports, after Spirit shut down in May 2026, JetBlue, Frontier, Breeze, and Allegiant all added capacity at Fort Lauderdale 1. JetBlue went after Spirit’s routes directly, launching 11 new Fort Lauderdale routes on Spirit’s shutdown weekend plus a status match for Free Spirit members 3. Allegiant took a different line: of its 42 Fort Lauderdale markets, only five — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City — were Spirit cities, and it is chasing unique markets instead 1.

    Industry observers note that that reflects the two models. Allegiant flies low-frequency leisure routes from smaller cities where it is often the only nonstop, so it avoids the daily-frequency, loyalty-driven markets JetBlue serves. JetBlue’s Fort Lauderdale is built around Northeast traffic, Caribbean and Latin connections — more than 20 routes to Latin America — and premium: Mint lie-flat on transcons to Los Angeles and Las Vegas, with management calling the city “Florida’s biggest premium market” 1. JetBlue is also adding its BlueFirst domestic first class and weighing a Fort Lauderdale lounge 4.

    Fort Lauderdale seats excluding Spirit were scheduled up a combined 40% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2026. If demand doesn’t absorb that, the thin unique routes Allegiant favors are the easiest to cut — and JetBlue, which is funding startup losses on new routes while chasing a turnaround, has the most capital at risk.

    This question was addressed to Sara Nelson, International President, Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO.

    Industry observers note that customer experience and labor-as-cost coexist only when the service promise matches the cost model. The carriers now cutting hardest — KLM, Icelandair, Alaska — are protecting margin under a fuel shock, not reinventing service. The real test is where the cuts land: outsourced ground and contact-center work, and regional crews paid about half mainline, is where the customer actually meets the airline. 326.

    Industry observers note that the fuel shock is forcing the trade-off into the open. Jet fuel was up 102% year over year in mid-September, and record revenue has not covered it 4. American grew revenue 19.3% in Q3 and still posted a 1% operating margin because costs grew 19.7%; Delta and United each slipped about two points 6. Carriers that already settled big contracts — United’s five-year flight attendant deal carries a 31% pay increase and $741 million in retroactive pay — are paying for premium service with loyalty and premium-cabin cash, not by squeezing crew 45.

    It has been revealed that the unresolved question is whether outsourcing the customer-facing layer — catering, ground handling, contact centers — reveals up in the service metrics airlines sell against. KLM has disclosed the cost target and the job moves; it has not disclosed a service standard tied to them.

    This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

    India’s fleet orders are not the binding constraint — ground and crew capacity are. Mumbai is rationing international slots to rebuild a terminal, newly introduced airports rather than bigger ones are being asked to absorb growth, and tighter pilot duty rules exposed how thin airline crew buffers were. The result: capacity now gets added where slots and crews exist, not where demand is. 1167.

    Industry observers note that mumbai International Airport told 46 airlines it would pull 265 of Terminal 2’s 770 weekly international departure slots from October 25 to house domestic flights displaced by the Terminal 1 rebuild — IndiGo losing 74 weekly departures, Air India 33, Emirates and Etihad 10 each 1. The ministry intervened, Adani agreed to leave winter slots untouched, and traffic balancing was pushed to the summer 2027 schedule 23. IndiGo and Air India Group then agreed to phase international flying to Navi Mumbai through July 2027 4. The relief valve carries its own friction: Navi Mumbai is 45 km away with no direct metro link expected before 2031, and charges INR 1,225 in passenger fees against INR 615 at Mumbai 4. Adani’s airport CEO expects one or two foreign carriers to suspend Mumbai service for a couple of years rather than split operations 5.

    Sources indicate that indiGo canceled more than 1,200 flights after new crew rostering rules collided with thin staffing and system congestion, and the DGCA opened a probe 6. The meltdown deepened — the government rolled back night-flying rules, capped fares, and fined the airline, and it cost IndiGo both profit and its CEO 789. The regulator has since shown it will flex duty rules when airspace disruption lengthens sectors, temporarily relaxing pilot duty-time limits in April 2026 10. Regulators also tied summer schedule approvals to aircraft actually on the ground rather than projected deliveries, forcing airlines to cut planned flying 11.

    In a recent development, skift’s reporting has tracked recruitment to beat an air traffic control officer shortage, with 796 ATC positions created alongside the fleet build-out 12, and CAPA has called for airspace redesign to carry 8–10 times current traffic 13. The sharper near-term airspace problem is geopolitical: Pakistani and Iranian closures pushed IndiGo to suspend Copenhagen and cut UK flying 14, and have hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, moving Air India’s Europe and North America flying toward Mumbai with Bengaluru under study as a third hub 15.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    The A220 is what makes Breeze’s network possible: small enough to open thin city pairs no one else serves, long-legged enough to fly them transcon, and cheap enough per trip that Breeze can sit on routes with no nonstop competition. The same airplane caps it. At 137 seats, its unit costs can’t match a densely configured A321neo, so Breeze can’t follow demand into massive, contested markets without losing the economics that work. 12.

    Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, according to Skift Research, and CEO David Neeleman estimates the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 2. He said Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — “that’s what got Spirit to die” — and pairs the smaller aircraft with premium seating and bundles to make thin routes work 23.

    Charleston, Providence, Hartford, Akron-Canton, Albany, Rochester, Memphis — cities where the Big Three lean on aging regional jets and rivals have pulled seats.

    The A220’s range lets Breeze link overlooked eastern cities to Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego, and Orange County, plus Las Vegas and Phoenix.

    Airline Weekly reported Breeze chases yield premiums instead, and avoids competing against densely configured narrowbodies.

    The A220 is a bet that U.S. majors keep upgauging and keep leaving mid-size cities to aging regional jets. That thesis has held. The risk arrives when Southwest’s 737 Max 7 — comparable in size and unit cost — finally shows up in volume, or when a thin market Breeze created attracts a larger airplane.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    The core of Porter’s 2021 case still stands: a 132-seat jet with low trip costs lets it hold daily frequency and keep fares up on routes bigger aircraft can’t fill profitably. What fuel has broken is the financing side. Jet fuel roughly doubled in 2026, Canada has lent money to Porter, Transat, and Flair, and the growth-at-pace ambition behind the 80-aircraft order now runs on borrowed room. 156.

    The original bet, made in July 2021, had three legs: the E195-E2 was picked over the A220 specifically for lower trip costs; its near-3,000-mile range opened nonstops other carriers only served via connections; and 132 seats against Air Canada and WestJet’s 169-174-seat 737-8s meant Porter could fly thinner markets 2. A fourth leg came with the 2022 product reveal — all-economy with PorterReserve, a premium-economy-light product, rather than following rivals downmarket 3.

    Fuel has not invalidated the aircraft choice — it has validated it. Smaller gauge is the right shape for a cost shock, because the fare you need per seat falls with the seats you have to sell. What fuel broke is the balance sheet assumption underneath the order: that Porter could scale a national network on its own money.

    Trip-cost economics and frequency — the revenue-side argument for small gauge is stronger at $4-plus fuel, not weaker 1.

    Self-funded expansion; Porter is now among the Canadian carriers taking government loans 5.

    Breeze, which protects economics with low trip costs and routes with limited nonstop competition 4.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    Low-cost carriers are genuinely loosening single-fleet discipline — AirAsia on regional jets, Avelo on the E2, IndiGo on widebodies. But slot scarcity isn’t the driver. The reporting points to revenue, not runway access: matching aircraft size to what a market will actually pay, and chasing premium and long-haul revenue the A320/737 can’t reach. Slot-constrained airlines do the opposite — they upgauge within one fleet. 123.

    The behavior behind the trend is real and spread across more than one region and one type of player. AirAsia’s Tony Fernandes is negotiating with Airbus and Embraer for regional jets, explicitly breaking from the single-type model to serve smaller destinations at higher frequency 2. Avelo ordered up to 100 Embraer E195-E2s alongside its all-Boeing 737 fleet, becoming the first U.S. carrier to commit to the type 3. IndiGo has 60 A350-900s on order, with the first now slipping to the second quarter of 2028 4. Flyadeal has weighed widebodies for high-volume pilgrim and worker routes 7.

    What those cases share is a revenue argument, not a capacity-access one. At Skift Aviation Forum, Embraer’s Arjan Meijer pointed to a widening gap between 76-seat regional jets and narrowbodies, and argued that lower per-seat costs can be wiped out by the revenue consequences of flying more seats than a market will absorb at a decent fare 1. Porter’s Kevin Jackson mentioned 132-seat E195-E2s let the airline hold daily service through weak periods and protect unit revenue 1.

    It has been revealed that slot constraints produce the opposite response: more seats through the same number of movements, inside one fleet type. EasyJet’s growth at slot-limited Gatwick, Linate, and Charles de Gaulle has come from upgauging A319s and A320s to A320neos and A321neos — roughly 171 seats to 211 — not from adding a second aircraft family 89. British Airways is cutting 52 economy seats per A380 to lift premium cabins to 48% of capacity at Heathrow, again raising revenue per slot rather than diversifying types 10. IndiGo’s A321XLRs on Athens and Amsterdam do protect slots, but that’s a secondary benefit of a long-haul product decision 4.

    Recent findings suggest that fleet simplicity still carries real weight. Cathay ruled out regional jets entirely, citing economies of scale and congested airports 6. Jackson remarked larger aircraft would suit some Porter routes, but a consistent E2 fleet serves the wider network strategy 1. And Willie Walsh has said IndiGo’s short-haul narrowbody core will not be reshaped to feed long-haul widebodies 5.

    If fuel stays elevated and fares keep deciding margins, more LCCs follow Avelo and AirAsia into a second, smaller type to defend yield in thin markets rather than dump seats into them.

    Mixed fleets raise crew, maintenance, and spares costs. If the carriers adding types can’t show unit-revenue gains that clear that bill, the discipline snaps back — Cathay’s reasoning becomes the consensus again.

    IndiGo’s model — a widebody arm run alongside an untouched narrowbody core — becomes the template for LCCs wanting long-haul without contaminating short-haul costs.

    Recent findings suggest that the single-fleet religion is loosening because LCCs are chasing revenue the A320 and 737 can’t capture — in thin markets and in premium and long-haul cabins. Slot scarcity pushes airlines toward bigger aircraft within one family, which is the opposite move.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    According to recent reports, skift’s reporting does not show a Porter proposal for replacing its Q400s at Billy Bishop. What the reporting does establish is the constraint that decides the answer: the tripartite agreement bars jets at the island airport, and Ottawa declined to reopen it in 2015, killing Porter’s CS100 order and runway-extension plan. Unless that agreement changes, anything Porter flies downtown has to be a turboprop. 12.

    Billy Bishop sits on an island in Lake Ontario with a runway of roughly 4,000 feet, restricted to turboprops — Porter’s Q400s already take a weight restriction to operate there 32. Porter’s growth since 2021 has gone the other way: up to 80 Embraer E195-E2s flown from Toronto Pearson, Montreal, Ottawa, and Halifax, with Billy Bishop kept as the separate downtown base 14. At Skift Aviation Forum this month, Porter President Kevin Jackson said a consistent 132-seat E2 fleet supports the airline’s network strategy, with smaller aircraft preserving frequency for business travelers through weaker periods 5.

    According to recent reports, the simplest path keeps Billy Bishop inside the existing rules: another regional turboprop type for the downtown operation, run alongside the E2 jet fleet. The cost is the fleet complexity Jackson remarked the airline has deliberately avoided.

    Jets downtown require a runway extension and a change to the agreement that governs the airport. Porter tried that in 2013 with a CS100 order and lost in 2015 when Ottawa declined to review it, with local opposition over noise and the waterfront.

    According to recent reports, porter’s jet network already runs from Pearson and eastern Canadian cities, and Billy Bishop’s value — a downtown gate and a U.S. preclearance facility — would have to be weighed against operating a second aircraft type for one airport.

    Whether the federal government reveals any willingness to revisit the tripartite agreement, and whether Billy Bishop’s U.S. preclearance facility — which Porter, as the airport’s only U.S. operator, stands to benefit from — raises the commercial value of staying downtown enough to justify a second fleet type 6.

    Porter’s downtown problem is a regulatory one, not a fleet one. Until the jet ban at Billy Bishop moves, Porter’s only options are another turboprop or a smaller presence on the island.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    According to recent reports, one U.S. carrier has ordered the E2: Avelo took 50 firm E195-E2s plus 50 purchase rights in September 2025. The reason no one else has is a weight limit written into major-airline pilot contracts. Scope clauses cap the maximum takeoff weight of jets regional partners may fly, and the re-engined E175-E2 is roughly 13,000 pounds over that line — so the aircraft that would sell in volume cannot legally be flown by the airlines that would buy it. 12.

    Sources indicate that the binding constraint is weight, not seats. Pilot union contracts at the big network carriers restrict the maximum takeoff weight of aircraft operated by regional partners; the E175-E2 comes in at about 99,000 pounds, well above what those contracts generally permit 2. Embraer’s Arjan Meijer called that threshold a “paper limitation” set years before anyone designed an E175 around Pratt & Whitney geared turbofans 2.

    Recent findings suggest that skyWest is the clearest casualty. It ordered 100 E175-E2s in 2013 on the expectation that scope would loosen; it never did, the order was not binding, and SkyWest kept buying first-generation E175s instead — including 20 more for American in early 2020 3. As of 2023, Embraer was still planning to build the older E1 alongside the E2 specifically because U.S. pilot contracts kept E1 demand alive 4.

    According to recent reports, the workaround is to skip the regional model entirely. Avelo is an independent ultra-low-cost carrier with no scope clause to satisfy, so it could order the larger E195-E2 outright, with deliveries from 2027 1. Porter Airlines in Canada has built a network on 132-seat E195-E2s, and its president Kevin Jackson argued at Skift Aviation Forum that the smaller gauge protects frequency and daily service through weak periods rather than chasing the lowest cost per seat 5.

    This question was addressed to Robin Hayes, Chairman and CEO of Airbus in North America, Airbus.

    Skift’s reporting doesn’t show an active ME3 campaign to relaunch the A380, and the conditions that would make Airbus say yes aren’t there. Emirates’ traffic fell 22% and its seat factor dropped to 72% in the half to September 30, with fuel at 34% of operating cost. A four-engine, 500-seat jet is the worst possible aircraft in a fuel shock. Airbus is sold out on the A350 instead. Likelihood: very low. 14.

    Recent findings suggest that the demand case the Gulf carriers once made for the A380 rested on slot-constrained airports and reliably full hubs. Both legs are weaker now. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers in the six months to September 30, down 22%, with capacity down 17% and seat factor at 72% from 79.5%, as the U.S.-Iran war pushed connecting traffic toward Istanbul and Singapore 1. Its first-half profit fell 66% to $899 million and survived only on $1.93 billion of hedging gains; analyst Linus Benjamin Bauer remarked the core flying business was likely loss-making unhedged 1. Emirates’ growth had already plateaued before the war on Dubai airport congestion, with FlyDubai taking the expansion role 5.

    What the Gulf carriers are actually buying is the answer. Emirates ordered 65 more Boeing 777Xs for $38 billion at the 2025 Dubai Airshow 2, holds more than 340 aircraft on order worth about $150 billion, and is spending more than $7 billion retrofitting existing jets rather than seeking new very-large aircraft 1. Etihad went the other way entirely, ordering 30 A321LRs and putting first class on a narrowbody 6. Qatar Airways’ Hamad Al-Khater stated the airline is working with Boeing on the delayed 777X and has 138 aircraft arriving over five years 9.

    In a recent development, airbus has the opposite problem to an empty line. Widebody demand is running hard into supply chain, labor, and production constraints, with the A350 backlog already deep 4. Restarting a closed four-engine program would compete for the same engineers, suppliers, and slots that Airbus is using to deliver aircraft it has already sold.

    Emirates has refitted aircraft inside a program valued at more than $7 billion, and British Airways is cutting its A380s from 469 to 417 seats to lift premium share to 48%. Existing airframes absorb premium demand without a new program.

    Fleet strategy debate has centered on a possible stretched A350 rather than a new superjumbo — a derivative Airbus can build on a line that is already running.

    Emirates added 65 777Xs for $38 billion and Qatar Airways notes it is working closely with Boeing on the delayed program. The large-twin answer is already ordered, just late.

    In a recent development, the A380 keeps its fans in the Gulf and at Heathrow, but the money is going into retrofits, twins, and narrowbodies. Airbus closed the line because the orders weren’t there, and a demand picture weaker than 2019’s doesn’t reopen it.

    This question was addressed to Darren Hulst, VP, Commercial Marketing, Boeing.

    Boeing’s delivery performance to Ryanair improved because Boeing slowed itself down first, then rebuilt the system around quality and regulatory sign-off. Ryanair’s complaints have shifted from defective, late aircraft to a more basic constraint: there aren’t enough slots.

    How Boeing’s Ryanair Deliveries Turned Around.

    O’Leary said only 40 of 57 expected 737 Max deliveries would arrive on time, forcing frequency cuts at high-cost airports.

    O’Leary said Max jets were arriving with fewer defects, citing better fuselages shipped from Wichita to Seattle, and asked Boeing for a blueprint to accelerate deliveries.

    The FAA acknowledged improvements in Boeing’s safety management, opening the door to higher 737 Max production, though delays still forced changes at Southwest and Ryanair.

    Airline Weekly cited improving Max deliveries and a widening unit-cost advantage as Ryanair headed into a strong peak summer.

    Boeing’s 737 chief Katie Ringgold mentioned traveled work was down about 60% in a year, suppliers were all at rate 42, and the next step to 47 a month would come in late spring or early summer 2026.

    Ryanair’s last 29 Gamechanger Max deliveries were each defect-free and arrived one to two months ahead of their revised dates, O’Leary stated, praising Kelly Ortberg and Stephanie Pope.

    Three things, all upstream of Ryanair.

    Quality control at the fuselage source. Spirit AeroSystems, which builds 737 Max fuselages in Wichita, was brought back inside Boeing. O’Leary flagged better fuselage quality as early as 2024, before the acquisition closed 32.

    Deliberate slowdown. Boeing cut output in 2024 to install stricter inspections and “move-ready” criteria. Ringgold remarked Boeing built fewer aircraft than customers needed as a result, and that those processes now show up as better quality and flow 2.

    The FAA became a gatekeeper. After the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout, the FAA capped 737 output at 38 a month and now formally approves every rate increase. Boeing was cleared to 42 in November 2025 2.

    It has been revealed that the improvement Ryanair is praising is partly an artifact of lowered expectations: those 29 aircraft arrived early against delivery dates that had already slipped by roughly a year. The durable gain is defect-free handover, which cuts Ryanair’s own acceptance and rework time.

    All of Ryanair’s Max 8s have been delivered. Its 300-aircraft Max 10 order is now the live question, with first delivery scheduled for spring 2027 and running through 2034 1. Boeing certified the Max 7 in August 2026 after about a decade of delays and was targeting Max 10 certification by year-end 7.

    It has been revealed that delivery reliability also matters more than usual right now. Ryanair cut its FY27 traffic target to 214 million passengers and reported a 15% drop in half-year profit after tax to €2.1 billion, with a €2 billion fuel bill increase coming in fiscal 2027/28 8. Newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft are one of the few cost levers that don’t require a fight with a union or an airport.

    This question was addressed to Juha Jaervinen, Chief Customer Officer, Virgin Atlantic.

    It has been revealed that british Airways’ A380 refit — 52 seats out, premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft — concentrates high-yield passengers behind a single slot at a Heathrow where BA can’t simply add a flight 1. Virgin Atlantic is running the same play at Heathrow, and started earlier: economy on refurbished 787s drops from 192 seats to 127, and latest A330s carry 104 premium seats against 128 in economy 34.

    In a recent development, doyle called it one of BA’s most significant aircraft transformations. IAG’s Gallego noted the heavier premium configuration would not work across every IAG market.

    Koster said Virgin had been underweight in premium since the A340-600 and called the shift an investment rather than a bet.

    Virgin has already chosen speed of conversion over amenity: the onboard bars, among its most recognizable brand assets, are being replaced with more spacious private seats 2. That is the cleanest counter to BA adding suites — Virgin converts the square footage it was spending on social space into sellable Upper Class.

    The second lever is the ground product, where Virgin is investing in the JFK Clubhouse and expanded Retreat Suites against BA’s upcoming Heathrow Terminal 5C lounge, due at the end of 2028 21. The third is the Delta joint venture, which Koster remarked gives Virgin network and scale while leaving the challenger brand intact 3.

    According to recent reports, virgin Atlantic isn’t being forced to respond to BA’s A380 refit — it moved first, and more aggressively relative to its fleet. The open question is yields: BA, Virgin, American, Alaska, Emirates, and Turkish are all adding premium seats into the same cycle, and Skift reporting flags crowding as the risk if supply grows faster than the pool of payers.

    This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

    Airlines control the single biggest lever for tier-2 and tier-3 growth — where they put seats. Crisil’s data highlights capacity deployment, not demand, is what turned Hindon and Kannur into million-passenger airports. But that lever only works where an airport, a usable aircraft type, and viability support already exist, and all three are government-set. Airlines can move the needle hard on existing regional airports; they can’t create the next 100. 12.

    In a recent development, regional airports make up 58% of India’s airports but carry just 2-3% of domestic traffic, and that share has gone backwards — from 3.4% in the 2021 and 2022 financial years to 2.3% in fiscal 2025 1. Crisil’s read is that the UDAN scheme’s importance has been “more structural than volumetric” 1. Where airlines did add capacity, the numbers moved fast: Hindon and Kannur each crossed 1 million annual passengers in fiscal 2025 on the back of increased deployment, and Agra, Hindon, and Tezpur grew traffic 7-10x between fiscal 2020 and 2025 against 120% national growth 1.

    According to recent reports, two things cap what airlines can do on their own. First, fleet: only about 80 dedicated regional transport aircraft fly in India, and the government projects a need for roughly 100 a year over the next decade 2. Narrowbodies don’t make 45-to-90-minute thin routes work. Second, economics: only about 5% of Indian domestic seat capacity sits on regional routes, compared with roughly double that in the U.S. and Europe, and 68% of domestic traffic touches one of the 10 busiest airports 8.

    The current cycle also works against small-city flying. IndiGo lost about INR 19 billion ($197 million) in the September quarter, with fuel up 67% against 26% revenue growth, and recovered only about 60% of the fuel increase through fares 5. Capacity under that pressure goes to dense trunk routes and international flying, not 70-seat regional hops. Akasa has named tier-2 and tier-3 cities as central to its domestic strategy 6, and Fly91 was built specifically for the gap 7, but neither carries the scale to change the national mix alone.

    Airlines decide whether India’s existing regional airports fill up — that is a real, provable lever worth multiples of traffic at individual airports. They do not decide whether the next tier of cities gets an airport, a subsidy, or an aircraft small enough to serve it profitably, and that is where the 2-3% national share is actually set.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    The single highest-impact move is closing the fuel-recapture gap — pricing and capacity discipline that turns a $4.64-a-gallon cost into fare revenue. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, so the premium bet can’t rescue 2027. JetBlue recaptured only 50% of fuel costs in Q2 2026, and it guided to a negative 4.5% to negative 6.5% operating margin. Fuel is where the margin went. 142.

    Everything else JetBlue is doing — premium cabins, Fort Lauderdale growth, lower-cost terminals, loyalty — matters, but on a slower clock. BlueFirst should add nearly five points of revenue per available seat mile, according to president Marty St. George, yet the retrofit doesn’t finish until late 2028 because of supply chain bottlenecks 31. The $1 EPS target assumes fuel near $3 a gallon; JetBlue paid $4.23 in Q2 2026 and expects $4.64 in Q4 42.

    Industry observers note that jetBlue has the right long-term strategy and the wrong timetable. The premium and loyalty build-out pays off in 2028; the fuel bill is due now, which makes pricing power and capacity cuts the only levers that move 2027.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Sources indicate that neither lever works alone. Fares recapture the cost only with a lag — United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3, below its own 80%-90% guidance. The carriers holding margin are pairing price with capacity discipline and revenue that doesn’t ride on a seat: premium mix, loyalty, cargo, and at Delta, a refinery. Operations decide who survives the lag. 15.

    According to recent reports, revenue at the six largest U.S. airlines rose about 18% year over year in the third quarter while operating profit was roughly flat 2. That gap is the whole argument: pricing is working, and it still isn’t enough on its own. Average domestic airfare is up about 32% year over year, per Kayak, and demand has held 3.

    The limits of the fare lever are clearest at Ryanair. Michael O’Leary said covering a €2 billion ($2.24bn) fuel increase through fares alone would need average ticket prices up about 20%, or €10 per passenger — and he doesn’t expect that, so Ryanair is targeting pay freezes, slower pilot recruitment, lower crewing ratios, and cheaper airport deals 4.

    Sources indicate that the deciding variable is the lag, not the lever. United’s CFO attributed the shortfall to the speed of the late-quarter spike rather than weak demand, and remarked United is highly confident it can recapture 100% — with a lag. Carriers with short booking curves reprice fast: Air Canada’s transborder unit revenue rose 24% year over year on close-in bookings while its longhaul passengers flew on fares booked before the spike. Operations buy the time that pricing needs.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Sources indicate that expect fares to rise again over the next year, though more slowly than the step-change of 2026. The driver is cost, not demand. Jet fuel hit record levels this year — September’s $4.37 a gallon U.S. average was an all-time high — and carriers have been passing it through 6. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs through pricing in Q3 and indicates it will close the gap to 100% next year, with a lag 6.

    It has been revealed that three forces point up. Scott Kirby is planning for elevated fuel through all of 2027 and argues fares are still below 2019 in real terms 6; he has stated airlines can pass the cost on, helped by Spirit’s collapse removing cheap domestic seats 8. American’s Robert Isom said there is more room to raise fares, and is slowing 2027 growth to protect profitability 6. Ancillaries are moving the same way — JetBlue raised bag fees twice in 2026 4.

    According to recent reports, two forces cap the increase. Capacity growth is picking up just as airlines push price, with weak consumer sentiment in the background, Melius Research’s Conor Cunningham warned 8. And the low-cost end can’t follow: Ryanair’s O’Leary said covering his fuel bill would need fares about 20% higher, said he doesn’t expect that, and is cutting costs instead 3.

    Europe is on a different clock. Hedges cushioned this year — Ryanair fares actually fell 2% in Q3 — but shorthaul fares inflected upward in August and are now modestly ahead of last year as carriers cut capacity, and the cheap hedges expire in 2027 12.

    This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

    Recent findings suggest that structurally higher fuel for three years doesn’t break demand — it breaks the weakest cost structures. Expect fares and fees to stay up, capacity growth to be rationed to routes that clear a higher hurdle, premium and loyalty to carry more of the P&L, and a thinning of unhedged, low-fare operators. United’s Scott Kirby is already planning for elevated fuel through all of 2027 and predicts weaker U.S. carriers will have to cut flying. 12.

    According to recent reports, the pass-through is real but slow. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in the third quarter, up from about 50% in the second and short of the 80%–90% it guided to over the summer, leaving roughly $500 million unrecovered in one quarter 1. Delta attributed its entire 2026 guidance cut — to $5.10–$``{=html}5.60 per share from $6.50–$``{=html}7.50 — to fuel, and about $6 billion in added expense this year 3. Over three years, that lag compounds into permanently repriced tickets: domestic airfares are already up about 30% this year 4.

    Industry observers note that three years of expensive fuel is a sorting mechanism, not a demand shock. Carriers with premium cabins, loyalty cash, and hedges reprice and keep flying; unhedged short-haul and low-fare operators cut, shrink fleets, or exit. IAG’s Luis Gallego remarked strong North Atlantic demand lets the group offset its fuel bill — that option isn’t available to everyone.

    This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

    Industry observers note that no single lever covers a fuel bill that doubled in 2026. Fares do most of the work — United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3, up from about 50% in Q2 — with capacity cuts, bag fees, premium and loyalty revenue, hedging, cargo, and labor cost closing the rest. Carriers with hedges, premium demand, or cargo are coping; those without are cutting flying. 91.

    Fuel averaged $4.41 a gallon in early November, and was 111% higher year over year in the week ending Oct. 9 311. Revenue at the six largest U.S. airlines rose about 18% in Q3 while operating profit was roughly flat 1.

    Raise faresDomestic airfare is up about 30-32% this year. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3 and expects a similar rate in Q4, having pushed back its 100% target; Q3 fuel rose $1.8 billion, leaving about $500 million unrecovered in one quarter. 3912.

    Cut capacityAmerican will slow 2027 growth, with Q4 capacity up 5.5-6.5% against roughly 2% at Delta and United. United indicates it will cut marginal routes; Ryanair cut its winter traffic target by two million passengers and European carriers trimmed capacity, which turned Q4 fares modestly positive. 10112.

    Ancillary feesJetBlue raised checked bag fees twice in 2026, to $50 from $45 for a first bag booked more than 24 hours out, and a spokesperson remarked the increase offsets rising fuel and operating costs while keeping base fares competitive. 3.

    Premium and loyalty mixPremium cabins produced 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion. United’s premium and loyalty revenue each rose 17% in Q3 and contracted business revenue rose 26%. IAG’s Luis Gallego said strong North Atlantic demand lets the group offset its fuel bill. 791.

    It has been revealed that hedgingEurope’s major groups absorbed the spike better because they are hedged — Ryanair at about 80% for the year to March 2027 at roughly $67abarrel.EmiratesstayedprofitableonlyonAED7.1billion($``{=html}1.93 billion) in hedging gains, which cut a 60% pre-hedge fuel increase to 13% net. Hedges expire: Ryanair is only 25% hedged at $95forthefollowingyearandfacesa€2billion($``{=html}2.24bn) fuel increase. 2134.

    According to recent reports, cut other costs, and sell cargoRyanair is targeting pay freezes, slower pilot recruitment, lower crewing ratios, cheaper airport deals, and more AI in back-office work, after O’Leary stated covering the gap on fares alone would need about 20% higher prices. Air Canada recaptured close to 100% of incremental fuel costs through cargo; Emirates’ SkyCargo revenue rose 52% on volumes down 1%. Alaska is cutting 200 back-office jobs. 4513.

    It has been revealed that the lever that decides outcomes is the booking curve, not the tactic. Air Canada’s transborder routes, which book close in, posted a 24% unit revenue surge, while longhaul passengers who booked 60 to 120 days out are flying on pre-spike fares. Recovery lags the price move, so the open question is how much further fares can rise before demand responds — IATA September traffic was down nearly 1% year over year. 5.

    This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

    Air India figures submitted to Indian officials; the airline has separately put the cost at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year.

    Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian carriers in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack, and the ban has been extended repeatedly 1. Nearly two years on, the economics are visible in three places: fuel burn, network design, and competitive position.

    Sources indicate that fuel and block time. Air India told Indian officials the closure pushed fuel costs up by as much as 29% and added up to three hours on some long-haul flights, costing roughly $455 million a year in profit before tax 1. In a separate accounting it put the figure at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year 2.

    Routes that no longer pay. Air India suspended Delhi–Washington in August 2025 and has struggled to run Mumbai– and Bengaluru–San Francisco efficiently 1. It cut or suspended services to North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia between June and August 2026, citing airspace restrictions and record jet fuel prices 5. IndiGo suspended Copenhagen and trimmed UK flying 6.

    Hub geography. The closure has hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, so CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said more Europe and North America flying moves to Mumbai, Delhi grows eastward, and Bengaluru is under study as a third hub 4.

    Competitive asymmetry. Foreign carriers that can still overfly Pakistan keep the shorter routings, which makes their nonstop and one-stop services out of India more competitive just as Air India and IndiGo build long-haul networks 1.

    In a recent development, the one live mitigation is a northern bypass. India has been negotiating with China for a corridor over Hotan in southern Xinjiang, which Air India estimated could cut its losses by about $1.13 million a week 1.

    Separating the airspace cost from the rest is hard. Fuel, the Iran war, and a weaker rupee are hitting at the same time, and IATA put Middle East airspace restrictions alone at 5–20% longer effective flight distances and roughly 2–10% higher operating costs on key Europe-Asia routes as of 2026.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Industry observers note that A Breeze IPO before late 2027 looks unlikely. Neeleman has already pushed his own target twice — from “a window in 2026” to 2027 — and the airline says it doesn’t need the capital, so a listing is about shareholder liquidity, not funding. Fuel is the gating factor: jet fuel doubled in 2026, U.S. carriers are cutting guidance, and airline equities are priced for that. Breeze can wait, and probably will. 325.

    Breeze is private and does not publish full financial results, so any read here rests on what Neeleman says publicly and on Skift’s reporting around it 1.

    In a recent development, jet fuel prices doubled in 2026, and airline pricing has not found a level that covers the increase — JetBlue President Marty St. George said as much in November 5. United recovered only 72% of its higher fuel costs in the third quarter and now plans for elevated fuel through all of 2027 6. Southwest cut 2026 earnings guidance to $2.60–$2.85 a share from $4, and Delta cut its range entirely on fuel 78.

    That matters for Breeze in three ways. Comparable valuations are depressed — Neeleman himself remarked airline stocks stay cheap because flying is discretionary spend and a leading indicator when confidence falls 3. The sector’s loss cases are loud: Frontier posted a $104 million net loss with an 82% jump in fuel costs, and JetBlue’s bonds traded at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 910. And Breeze’s own cushion is structural rather than hedged — low trip costs, 80% to 90% self-generated traffic, and sole-operator status on nearly 90% of its routes, which gives it pricing room most low-cost carriers lack 111.

    Breeze has the profit record an IPO needs and none of the urgency. With fuel suppressing airline multiples into 2027, the rational move is to keep compounding profitable quarters privately and list when the sector re-rates — which argues for late 2027 at the earliest.

    Industry observers note that what would pull it forward: a sustained drop in jet fuel — the Argus U.S. jet fuel index already fell 13% from $4.90 a gallon on Oct. 22 to $4.27 — combined with a full year of audited profitability and a clean story around the new Priceline-style ground-commerce revenue Neeleman wants to start next year 131.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Breeze’s IPO Timeline, As Told by Its CEO.

    Breeze posted its first operating profit, in Q4 2024, with revenue up 78% year over year.

    Neeleman told Skift an IPO could come as soon as 2026 if equity markets rebounded, but stated Breeze doesn’t need the capital — a listing would mostly give existing shareholders liquidity.

    At Skift Aviation Forum, Neeleman stated Breeze expected profitability the following year and now saw an IPO in 2027 rather than 2026.

    Airline Weekly noted Breeze was still chasing annual profitability nearly five years after launch.

    At Skift Aviation Forum, Neeleman said Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, and margins ‘in the top tier of the industry.’ He discussed a new Priceline-style revenue model rather than a listing.

    The last public date Neeleman put on a Breeze listing was 2027, set at Skift Aviation Forum in December 2025, after he pushed it back from 2026 2. He has not updated that timeline in Skift’s reporting since. At this month’s Skift Aviation Forum he talked about profitability, premium seat mix, AI staffing, and a proposal to clip a commission on the economic activity Breeze creates in small markets — not about going public 1.

    What has changed is the financial case. Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full results, but Neeleman remarked it has now strung together four profitable quarters with a fifth expected, and that margins are in the top tier of the industry 1. That is the record a filing would need, and a sharp turn from a year ago, when Airline Weekly was still writing about Breeze’s struggle to reach annual profitability nearly five years after launch 5.

    One more consideration: Neeleman is building toward a revenue model that looks less like an airline — taking a cut of real estate and hospitality spending in markets Breeze opens, with first steps expected next year 1. A manufacturer mid-pivot on how it makes money has a reason to wait until that line is proven before pricing itself for public investors.

    This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

    Not worth it as a package. Finnair is the only strategic fit — and Helsinki’s 50.1% floor means it isn’t for sale. Air Europa is the asset IAG already tried and abandoned after Brussels signaled a block. Norwegian is a Nordic short-haul and package-holiday group IAG has no playbook for. IAG’s own capital discipline argues against all three: Gallego funds projects that beat a 12-15% group margin bar, and these would not. 128.

    Each target fails on different grounds, and the failures don’t offset each other.

    Finnair is the one with real logic. Skift reported a decade ago that IAG was seen as a likely buyer, with Helsinki a counterbalance to London, Madrid, and Dublin 4. That case has weakened. The 2022 closure of Russian airspace severed the Siberian shortcut that made Helsinki-to-Asia profitable, and Finnair is still rebuilding around the wound 1. The Finnish state owns about 55% under a mandate to hold at least 50.1% 1. Finnair also already sits with British Airways and Iberia in a transatlantic joint business, which gives IAG little reason to buy what it already flies with 1. Finnair raised its full-year profit forecast in October on stronger-than-expected demand, so the discount is narrowing anyway 7.

    According to recent reports, air Europa is settled history. IAG abandoned the €400 million deal in August 2024 after EU regulators signaled they would likely block it, even after IAG offered to cede more than half of Air Europa’s flights \[\[cite:skn_697884\],\[cite:aw_39375\]\]. IAG would have held close to two-thirds of Madrid seats 6. Nothing in the competitive math has changed, and Turkish Airlines took a minority position in Air Europa last year 1.

    Norwegian is the weakest fit. It is in expansion mode, not up for sale — it bought Widerøe and then agreed to acquire Nordic Leisure Travel Group for about $843 million, lifting group revenue nearly 50% to roughly $6.3 billion \[\[cite:skn_828929\],\[cite:skn_824113\]\]. That is a vertically integrated package-holiday business in the TUI and Jet2 mold 3, not the premium long-haul hub model IAG runs.

    Sources indicate that finnair’s value to IAG already flows through the transatlantic joint business and a Japan partnership. Extending commercial agreements captures most of the network benefit without a Helsinki negotiation or a Brussels review.

    Gallego reviews airline investment proposals twice a year and funds what delivers the strongest shareholder returns against a 12-15% group margin target. Iberia hit a 16.4% operating margin in 2025 on refleeting and A321XLR transatlantic expansion — organic returns IAG controls.

    Sources indicate that europe’s distressed assets move on their own terms. Condor’s owner Attestor has openly sought a partner, and airBaltic needed a state loan in April 2026. A smaller, cheaper target clears regulators more easily than a three-way Nordic-Iberian package.

    Recent findings suggest that IAG is the most profitable European legacy group and does not need to buy scale it can’t integrate. The one target worth having is the one it can’t buy.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    JetBlue can avoid both a merger and Chapter 11, but the margin for error is thin. It has $2.2 billion in liquidity and about $7 billion in unencumbered assets, enough to fund the JetForward initiative through a fuel spike. What it does not have is a buyer — United’s CFO just ruled itself out on JetBlue’s $10 billion debt load — or a second year of negative margins. 12.

    Survival here is an arithmetic, not a strategy problem. JetBlue has lost money for six straight years and guided 2026 to an adjusted operating margin of negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, cut from negative 2% to negative 5% 2. Third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $2.8 billion, and it still posted a $257 million net loss 24. The cause is fuel: $4.64 a gallon expected in the fourth quarter against $3.91 in the third, while the $1 EPS target assumes fuel near $3 24.

    The bond market has already priced the risk. Debt maturing by 2031 traded at a record-low 40 cents on the dollar in October, down from about 80 cents earlier that month, and senior creditors hired PJT Partners and Akin Gump Strauss to discuss a restructuring 3. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and what our financial results are demonstrating” 3.

    The key uncertainty is fuel, not demand. JetBlue’s premium and cost levers are working — Q3 revenue grew 21%, BlueFirst should add nearly five points of unit revenue, and $30 million of controllable costs came out in the quarter — but none of that closes a gap created by paying $4.64 a gallon. If 2027 fuel lands near the slightly-above-$4 JetBlue assumes rather than $3, the EPS target slips and creditors, not management, set the calendar.

    This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

    The conditions that made IndiGo have closed. IndiGo and Air India now hold nearly 90% of domestic capacity, and IndiGo’s own scale — 550+ aircraft and 200 million passengers targeted by 2030 — is the floor Akasa would have to clear. Akasa’s realistic path is a profitable third carrier built on Southeast Asia and secondary routes, not a challenger for the domestic crown. 12.

    It has been revealed that indiGo’s win came from being the disciplined low-cost operator in a market of first-time flyers, capturing roughly two-thirds of the world’s third-largest domestic market 34. That pool of unserved demand is now largely spoken for. India’s domestic market is more concentrated than at any point in its modern history, with IndiGo and Air India holding close to 90% of capacity 1.

    Akasa’s constraints are the ones IndiGo never faced at the same stage: airport capacity limits, restrictive bilateral rights, and a post-pandemic talent shortage 5. Narrowbody delivery slots are scarce until roughly 2033, which caps how fast any latest entrant can add metal 6.

    It has been revealed that akasa’s one clear advantage right now is network choice. When the Iran war froze Gulf expansion, it redirected to Southeast Asia, adding Mumbai–Hanoi as its seventh international destination and building on Phuket 78. In the first full quarter after the war began, Indian carriers’ international traffic fell about 27% overall, while Akasa grew 26% 9.

    Recent findings suggest that the open question is whether Akasa can fund sustained growth through a high-fuel cycle. IndiGo lost about INR 19 billion ($197 million) in the September quarter with fuel up 67% against 26% revenue growth, recovering only about 60% of the fuel increase in fares. A subscale carrier absorbing the same shock has less room than the market leader.

    Trump signs bill to halt penny production

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that president Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday.
    • The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.
    • The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that president Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

    The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.

    “Washington has a spending problem, and it shows up in places big and small,” the bill's sponsor, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., mentioned Friday in a statement released by the office of House Financial Services Chairman French Hill, R-Ark. “If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken.”.

    Hill said in the statement that the bill also provides "clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers," referring to the measure's requirements that cash transactions not settled with exact change will be rounded to the nearest nickel.

    The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies a year ago under an executive order. Pennies already in circulation will still be legal tender, and the Mint may still issue special collectors editions. The legislation, named the Common Cents Act, also sets composition specifications for nickels.

    Industry observers note that like a well-traveled coin, the bill itself took a winding road to the White House. The House originally passed a similar bill in July and the Senate passed its version by unanimous consent on Aug. 7.

    According to recent reports, but the Senate added a section that would require the Treasury secretary to notify Congress before discontinuing other coins. That sent the bill back to the House with a Senate number.

    In a recent development, as the sponsor of the original measure, McClain insisted that the legislation have a House bill number. So, she reintroduced the revised Senate version, and the House voted on it on Sept. 14. The Senate passed it once again by unanimous consent on Sept. 28, sending it to the president's desk.

    Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., noted the bill “modernizes our currency system and most importantly gives families and businesses clear rules for everyday cash transactions.”.
