    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.
    • In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.
    • The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

    In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

    The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

    Industry observers note that that means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

    Recent findings suggest that in South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

    Sources indicate that democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

    In a recent development, democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

    In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

    Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the fresh lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

    Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

    Industry observers note that after Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with newly introduced congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

    Recent findings suggest that with GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

    According to recent reports, under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

    Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

    Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

    Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

    Industry observers note that the tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

    Industry observers note that and one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

    Democrats call for chip export and AI limits as Huang returns

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is among Democrats looking to take a harder line on AI and chip exports in the new year.
    • Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
    • The issue also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh aims to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is among Democrats looking to take a harder line on AI and chip exports in the new year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

    Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

    The issue also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh aims to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.

    The reinstatement of Huang came as President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday the CEO “did nothing wrong” and that he had been “speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly.”.

    Sources indicate that in a Monday statement, Nvidia stated its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

    Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader role, told reporters Monday that in the “first 100 days” of the latest Congress, he wants Senate rules changed to allow for faster floor consideration of bills that had broad bipartisan support in committee.

    He also supports legislation to require independent mandatory evaluations of AI systems and updates to liability laws to account not just for harm caused by AI models but for risks of internal development. He also mentioned a bill he sponsored that he said would ensure other electricity consumers don’t bear the costs of data center construction.

    Van Hollen also said that Congress should create a special joint committee on AI to consider the technology’s broader impacts, including on the workforce and economy.

    “I think we need to move urgently on the safety piece and then move with deliberation, but also speed, on tackling these other concerns,” Van Hollen said.

    Last week, Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., wrote to Van Hollen and Schumer proposing a joint committee to “complement” the work of committees of jurisdiction and asking for their plans for AI if they were elected leader.

    Recent findings suggest that speaking to reporters and in his reply to Hickenlooper, Van Hollen also supported greater transparency into the AI industry’s financing and debt structure and tighter export controls on advanced chips like those sold by Nvidia. In particular, he mentioned the Commerce Department should close “loopholes” for remote access to chips and purchase by affiliates of companies banned from directly acquiring sensitive technologies.

    Schumer, in a post on X Monday, remarked Democrats would “work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.”.

    “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer wrote.

    In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., whose caucus officially backed him last week to be speaker in the new year, seconded the need for investigations into Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He also supported export controls.

    “The National Defense Authorization Act must include ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries,” Jeffries wrote, referring to the pending fiscal 2027 defense policy bill.

    According to recent reports, A manager’s amendment to the Senate’s version of the bill includes several chip export restrictions, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House-passed NDAA does not contain similar language.

    Meanwhile, Republican committee leaders pressed forward with prepares to bring in Huang for questioning.

    Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., on Monday confirmed plans for a Dec. 3 hearing titled “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls” featuring Huang as a witness.

    "Mr. Huang’s testimony before the Senate Banking Committee will be critical for protecting America’s AI advantage,” Scott noted in a statement. “The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing.".

    Recent findings suggest that scott previously invited Lutnick to testify before the committee on Dec. 10.

    Sources indicate that sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who looks likely to hold the banking gavel next Congress, said Huang’s return as CEO “only increases the urgency” of export controls.

    According to recent reports, “The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the tech giant’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren remarked in a statement.

    In a recent development, house Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., said in a social media video on Monday that Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter would sit for transcribed interviews with his committee and with the House Intelligence Committee and Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party the week of Nov. 30.

    The committees also requested that Commerce Undersecretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler appear before the panels.

    John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

    Breaking: Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that for all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some notable lessons.
    • Recent findings suggest that that latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit.
    • Waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that for all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some notable lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

    Recent findings suggest that that latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

    Waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”.

    Industry observers note that reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”).

    Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

    Not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

    It has been revealed that but this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

    For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a newly introduced project after a string of flops.

    If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

    What Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

    It has been revealed that but it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Recent findings suggest that what’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion demonstrates maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

    If America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. In last month’s companion piece to “The Social Network,” Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his director’s eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. “I’m worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts you can’t learn,” he admitted.

    While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkin’s introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person claims so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

    For me, those are pre-shredded cabbage and carrots.

    Cook some small pasta â Iâm fond of cubetti here â and add frozen peas and carrots, cooking them just long enough to heat through. Drain, cool slightly and toss with canned white beans and a generous amount of Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto.

    Remember those Whole Foods chicken cutlets I was raving about earlier? Hereâs one of my favorite things to do with them.

    Sources indicate that the result is creamy, tangy, savory, crunchy and a little peppery. Itâs the sort of sandwich Iâd happily pay a cute restaurant a slightly unreasonable amount of money to make for me.

    Instead, Iâm standing in my own kitchen, feeling very pleased with myself.

    #146635. Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a new tune to follow.
    • On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.
    • The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a new tune to follow.

    On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

    The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

    It has been revealed that voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

    Recent findings suggest that trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

    In the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

    Industry observers note that over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

    According to recent reports, critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

    Sources indicate that trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on key commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

    Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

    In a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

    Albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

    But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

    According to recent reports, like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

    In a recent development, political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

    The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

    The election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

    But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

    Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

    An election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Recent findings suggest that the Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more notable than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

    When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.
    • The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table.
    • And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

    The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in Upcoming Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

    And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

    In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

    It has been revealed that put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

    That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

    Sources indicate that but here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

    In a recent development, this is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

    It has been revealed that I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

    So I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    According to recent reports, the refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of Fresh Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just remarked for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

    Chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a new one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

    It has been revealed that for those of us in Britain who care about democracy, November 20 marked a disturbing political development that Americans should take notice of. Prime Minister Andy Burnham traveled to Brussels for the U.K.-EU Summit — a renegotiation of Britain’s trading terms with the EU. Standing alongside the European Union’s chief bureaucrats, Burnham announced a series of deals — concentrating on food standards, youth mobility between Britain and the EU, and carbon and energy trading — that will erect fresh trade barriers between the U.K. and the United States.

    In June 2016, over 17 million Britons voted to leave the European Union and take back control of our lawmaking abilities from Brussels. The principle of parliamentary sovereignty — the foundation of the British constitution, which holds that Parliament is the supreme lawmaking authority in the land — had been eroded during our membership in the EU as we increasingly outsourced decision-making to unelected foreign bureaucrats. The Brexit vote was a watershed in British politics that allowed us to become the sovereign state we are today.

    Joseph Dinnage is senior press officer at the Prosperity Institute.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Industry observers note that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people.
    • In a recent development, when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

    Industry observers note that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

    In a recent development, when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

    Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

    Industry observers note that the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

    The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

    Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

    Industry observers note that thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

    • Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., pictured leaving the Capitol on Nov. 9, will resign Dec. 1. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec. 1 after the House Ethics Committee remarked it found “substantial evidence” that Gomez engaged in sexual misconduct with a congressional staffer.

    Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, announced his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also noted Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.

    The report was one of four released by the Ethics panel Monday. Three of them are about members who are set to depart the House after the 119th Congress, and the fourth is about the conduct of a former chief of staff.

    In a statement, Gomez said he took “full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” but that he also had “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.” Despite his concerns with the process, though, he said he saw no alternative other than to resign because “he was not given an opportunity to respond” to the final report.

    A statement issued by lawyers representing the female staffer with whom Gomez was accused of engaging in misconduct applauded the “thorough and sensitive” handling of the investigation.

    It has been revealed that “However, Representative Gomez’s conduct did not occur in a vacuum, and immediate steps must be taken by Congress to rein in what the report describes as a ‘toxic and predatory culture,’” the attorneys, Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt, added. “Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service.”.

    In a recent development, the committee began investigating Gomez after a New York Post story alleged the congressman was seen kissing a congressional staffer at a party hosted by then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif. At the time, Gomez mentioned he did not violate any House ethics rules. Swalwell resigned earlier this year amid a slew of sexual assault allegations from four separate women, one of whom was a former staffer.

    It has been revealed that but the more serious allegations addressed by the Ethics probe involve another female staffer, identified in the report as Witness 1. She testified in a deposition with the committee that on one occasion, Gomez touched her genitals without consent at a Washington bar. Gomez mentioned in his own interview with the committee that while he did engage in sexual conduct with the staffer, “she did not say no, she did not push me away.”.

    The same staffer, who did not work for Gomez, said he made inappropriate advances in a separate incident in Gomez’s congressional office, which Gomez downplayed as just a “beso,” or kiss, and hug.

    In its report, the committee determined that the congressional staffer’s testimony “was clear and was supported by evidence that she contemporaneously complained of his conduct” to another witness, and was part of an intolerable “toxic and predatory culture” on Capitol Hill.

    A statement issued by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other House Democratic leaders called the report “serious and deeply troubling,” and that Gomez’s resignation was “appropriate.”.

    “Decisive action to set a upcoming standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” the statement stated.

    It has been revealed that gomez was one of two House members from the Golden State to lose to a fellow Democrat earlier this month. Northern California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones.

    Gomez faced off against Angela Gonzales-Torres in the general election after both advanced from the state’s all-party primary in June. Gonzales-Torres, a Democratic Socialist and housing advocate, had the backing of several progressive groups, including Justice Democrats and Leaders We Deserve. Her supporters criticized Gomez after the House Ethics panel opened its investigation in August. Her campaign also sought to publicize the inquiry in the weeks leading up to Election Day, The Washington Post reported.

    In a recent development, the committee also released findings of its probes into Reps. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and Troy Nehls, R-Texas, as well as Brandon Phillips, Collins’ former chief of staff.

    Collins, who lost his Senate bid earlier this month, was under review following an Office of Congressional Conduct referral alleging that Phillips hired his girlfriend as an intern. Collins’ lawyers denied the allegations, and Phillips was fired earlier this year.

    Collins and the committee reached a mutual agreement under which he would return $2,880 to the U.S. Treasury after the committee found he had overpaid the “intern,” allowing it to close the case.

    Phillips, who did not comply with his congressional subpoenas, has been recommended by the committee to be held in contempt of Congress.

    Recent findings suggest that “At no point did Mr. Phillips offer a satisfactory legal justification for his failure to comply with the subpoena,” the committee wrote.

    It has been revealed that the committee probed Nehls for allegedly using campaign money for his personal benefit. Nehls did not run for reelection, but his twin brother, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, will replace him in January.

    The committee found that the Texas Republican “improperly used a firm that he owned as a political committee; the company, Liberty 1776, received and disbursed funds for the benefit of Representative Nehls’ campaign and other unverifiable purposes.”.

    Daniela Altimari contributed to this report.

    To relieve stress nowadays, modern high school students may fire up a game of Grand Theft Auto VI or bring a puppy dog to class. But in the recent past, American high schools would set aside a patch of blacktop where tense teenagers could fire up a couple of heaters between classes, presumably so nobody would show up to fourth-period algebra in nicotine withdrawal. Understanding that there was nothing they could do to prevent kids from lighting up, schools in the 1970s and 1980s frequently had smoking courts. The calculation was that they might as well keep the students in their line of sight.

    In those days, airplane passengers could light up while in flight, swathing 150 strangers inside a metal tube at 30,000 feet in Pall Mall smoke from Milwaukee to Phoenix.

    It has been revealed that the upcoming era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

    What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

    The fresh era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

    Sources indicate that what does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

    Industry observers note that the Horn’s littoral states cannot wish away geography or the incentives that it creates. But they do have room to maneuver. Robust public debate among Horn publics, prudent decision-making from ruling elites, and conscientious engagement from key external partners can ensure that this upcoming chapter of geopolitical centrality does not further destabilize a region that is already at the precipice.

    According to recent reports, the Horn of Africa has been a critical node since the inauguration of the Suez Canal in 1869. But the intensity with which this fact has been felt has waxed and waned over time. The start of the Yemen War in 2015 initiated another period of growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and a range of outside powers, each of whom sought a strategic perch near the Red Sea corridor from which to project their security and commercial interests.

    But the turmoil in the  Middle East after Oct. 7, 2023, has sharpened this dynamic. Two developments have been particularly consequential. The first is the Houthi campaign to interrupt maritime traffic in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, with a first wave of attacks beginning in November 2023 and a second wave targeting Saudi shipping starting in the summer of 2026. The second dynamic has been the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East. Although these respective blocs are not entirely coherent, there are clear divisions over Israel’s increasingly muscular security policy; the Iran crisis; and their respective interventions in conflicts between national governments and subnational armed actors across the region.

    In the face of fresh strategic pressures, several extra-regional actors have sought enhanced access and position in this zone, over and above what they had secured in preceding years. A triumvirate of littoral countries/de-facto states have been immediate targets: Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea.

    In a recent development, the impact is most apparent in Somaliland. Its economic partnership with the UAE, through the latter’s investment in the Berbera corridor, is long-standing. But this relationship has become increasingly securitized since 2024. The clearest evidence is what transpired at Berbera Airport, which has come under the effective security control of the UAE. Satellite imagery suggests the construction of an adjoining dock and the hardening of the airport’s infrastructure, including the development of underground bunkers that are potentially for ammunition and fuel. Many believe the airport has also become a logistical node in the UAE’s broader military supply network across East Africa, enabling the delivery of weapons to Sudan and Ethiopia.

    In a recent development, israel’s expanding role in Somaliland has run in parallel with the growing Emirati military presence. Israel diplomatically recognized Somaliland in December 2025—making it the first country in the world to do so—and some reports suggest an active Israeli intelligence presence in Berbera and the use of the airport for refueling its jets during the Iran war. Somaliland officials generally do not confirm these reports but acknowledge that an Israeli military presence is an eventual possibility.

    In a recent development, A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in Hargeisa, Somaliland, on Oct. 16. Mohamed Ahmed/Reuters.

    Recent findings suggest that washington has also joined the club. In the last year, Somaliland has hosted the commanding generals of AFRICOM and SOCAFRICA. A number of U.S. military personnel based at the Baledogle Airfield in Somalia have now been redeployed to Somaliland, prompting one senior Somaliland official to privately quip, “Team Mogadishu has now become Team Hargeisa.” U.S. training opportunities for Somaliland’s security forces appear to have also grown. These developments are still nascent and as such do not yet involve the deployment of critical intelligence, security, and reconnaissance capabilities, but the direction of travel is fairly clear.

    Sources indicate that the Emirati government’s formula in Puntland has largely tracked its approach to Somaliland. Beginning in the 2010s, the Emirati footprint in the statelet had mostly consisted of a commercial port concession in Bosaso and training Puntland’s Maritime Security Forces. But from 2024 onward, the UAE scaled up its activity in Bosaso, turning an airbase next to the civilian airport into another logistical hub through which weapons, ammunition, and personnel flowed to Emirati allies throughout the Horn. The UAE has also supported Puntland’s 2024-2025 offensive against Islamic State contingents in the region through direct drone strikes. The United States has also directly backed counter-Islamic State military operations, and according to Puntland authorities, agreed in August 2026 to establish a military facility at the same Bosaso airbase that houses an Emirati presence.

    In a recent development, eritrea’s incorporation into this picture looks a bit different. Its external alignments sharply diverge from Somaliland and Puntland, and there is presently no evidence that Eritrea is poised to play host to foreign military facilities. Yet if the past is prologue, then Eritrea could soon find itself housing a more significant military presence. There are unconfirmed reports of the potential for an increased Egyptian presence in the southern port of Assab. Assab served as the logistical fulcrum of Emirati military operations in Yemen, and back in the early 2000s, the Eritrean government lobbied the United States to establish a military base in Eritrea. At the time, Washington declined the Eritrean offer and established its premiere African military base in neighboring Djibouti.

    According to recent reports, people sail past container ships anchored near the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Aug. 6. AFP via Getty Images.

    Sources indicate that maritime exigencies in and around the Bab el-Mandeb have now pushed Eritrea higher on the Trump administration’s agenda. While U.S.-Eritrea relations have been relatively poor for more than two decades, Washington allowed a Tigray-related sanctions package targeting the Eritrean government to expire in September 2026. This was a clear bid to enhance relations with Asmara and was tied to a broad, if not clearly defined, sense that Eritrea mattered for Red Sea security. This sanctions removal occurred even though some notable U.S. policymakers believed that Eritrea had not really done enough to warrant such action.

    Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea will probably extract clear strategic rewards from their emerging geopolitical centrality and the related expansion of security partnerships. All three face increasingly acute security dilemmas from what they regard as revanchist neighbors and their respective external backers. All of their national political projects are also at critical junctures: Somaliland is attempting to build momentum for wider recognition; Puntland is maneuvering to protect its autonomy within a Somali federation; and Eritrea is working to fully break its political estrangement from much of the international system. Somaliland and Puntland have even leveraged the good offices of Abu Dhabi and Washington to improve a bilateral relationship long riddled with tension.

    People participate in a rally to celebrate the Houthis’ takeover of the strategic port city of Mocha and the Bab el-Mandeb strait in Sana’a, Yemen, on Sept. 11. Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images.

    The risks, however, are very real. The first is that these small polities quickly find themselves entrapped in conflicts that are not their own. The concern is most relevant to Somaliland, where the intensification of the Emirati, Israeli, and U.S. security presence is clearest. Though Houthi attacks in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have had negative economic repercussions on Berbera port, Somaliland’s authorities have no interest in getting involved in a regional war against the Houthis. But they might not have a choice. The Houthis themselves have threatened to strike any Israeli military presence in Somaliland and even hacked the website of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in early July. If a conflict led to missile or drone strikes on Berbera, it would have a catastrophic impact on trade, government revenue, and oil imports.

    According to recent reports, there is also a risk that Somaliland’s deepening security engagement with the Abraham bloc alienates it from Saudi Arabia, which is clearly unnerved by the growing security presence of the Emiratis and Israelis in the southern Red Sea. Somaliland’s critical livestock export sector, which provides 80 percent of all export earnings, is oriented toward the Saudi market, meaning it can ill afford to antagonize Riyadh.

    In a recent development, somaliland’s authorities are no doubt hoping to manage the scale and conduct of the foreign military element within its borders, so as to not provoke retaliation from actors they otherwise have few differences with. Although not widely known, when it was negotiating a memorandum of understanding for sea access with Ethiopia in late 2023, Somaliland placed real limitations on an Ethiopian naval presence in its Gulf of Aden shores. This included the denial of a land corridor between the Ethiopian border and naval base, as well as limits on the Ethiopian military’s interactions with local communities and third-party military activity. But does Somaliland have the autonomy to fully constrain what Israel, the UAE, and the United States do within its borders?

    According to recent reports, the second risk is that external actors’ push for newly introduced Red Sea-oriented partnerships might inadvertently fuel escalatory dynamics in the region. This is most evident in the growing tensions between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The scramble for positions along the Horn’s Red Sea littoral has provided landlocked Ethiopia a new set of justifications to press its maritime claims, including to the port of Assab in Eritrea. Ethiopian officials have argued that since the Red Sea and its Horn ports are increasingly contested terrain, an Ethiopian naval presence is the only way to ensure the country’s economic and security interests. They also make the point that if it is legitimate for outside powers to establish military bases along the Red Sea littoral, then it is an equally legitimate course of action for Ethiopia.

    In a recent development, A view of U.S. military aircraft at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti on Jan. 21, 2024. Djibouti sits opposite Yemen, across the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and between Eritrea and Somaliland.Getty Images.

    In a recent development, at the same time, U.S. sanctions removal, and the growing proximity between Cairo and Asmara, has increased Eritrea’s willingness to risk conflict with its southern neighbor. Indeed, the decision by the TPLF and the Alliance for Survival to launch offensives on Sept. 23, likely with the approval of Asmara, came just six days after the U.S. sanctions regime on Eritrea expired.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile, Emirati-Israeli involvement in Somaliland and Puntland has further consolidated Mogadishu’s increasing all-weather alliance with Turkey. President Hassan Sheikh has used Somalia’s growing defense partnerships with Turkey, which has deployed F-16s to the region to fight Al-Shabaab, to put pressure on Somaliland and Puntland. Most recently, this has involved an electronic visa scheme managed by Mogadishu to control the movement of foreign passport holders into Somaliland, and a reported agreement with Ankara to build a military base in Laasqoray, which sits in territory that Somaliland considers its own.

    Analysts fear that the renewed conflict could quickly draw in other regional actors.

    How Washington bargains away its Africa strategy to other regions.

    In a recent development, as a result, the risk of conflict between Mogadishu, Garowe, and even Hargeisa has increased considerably. In July and August, for instance, there were military confrontations between Puntland’s government and the Puntland Security Force, a militia that had increasingly come under the sway of Mogadishu, resulting in the PSF bases in Galkayo and Bosaso being seized by Puntland authorities.

    A final risk is related to the core governance questions that will shape the regional security landscape of the Horn in the coming years.

    Sources indicate that consider Eritrea, which has been mired in a deep human rights crisis for decades. This has driven hundreds of thousands of its young people abroad and produced deep, if still suppressed, social fissures. The country has no functioning constitution or electoral system, and thus no mechanism for peacefully navigating succession or adjudicating domestic political differences. Its political elite, in power since 1991, is unwilling to cultivate younger leaders or embrace basic economic and political reforms, offering little more than time-worn cliches about the need to defend against sabotage by external enemies. Unsurprisingly, U.S. sanctions relief engages none of these complications.

    In a recent development, in Somaliland and Puntland, the problem is one of political polarization, as deepening external partnerships have widened disagreements between contending political factions. Somaliland’s recognition deal with Israel has drawn internal criticism, including from religious actors, on both moral and strategic grounds. This was particularly true after Hargeisa made the controversial decision to place its embassy in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv in July. In Puntland, some opponents of President Saeed Deni believe he is using Emirati patronage to further consolidate his power. In all of these debates and more, fairly explosive clan rivalries lurk just beneath the surface.

    Members of the Somaliland Coast Guard participate in a parade in Hargeisa on May 18. Kang-Chun Cheng/AFP via Getty Images.

    Sources indicate that the Horn’s littoral states can navigate the risks associated with their emerging geopolitical centrality. But it will require more than business as usual. The first step is robust public debate about the risks and rewards of external security entanglements, so that all relevant considerations are surfaced. In many ways, Somaliland is ahead of the curve in this regard, a reflection of its relatively strong—although far from perfect—democratic system.

    Ruling elites must also prudently assess the costs and benefits of foreign basing and military cooperation. The challenge here is that the democratic deficit in some of these states means that regime security often prevails over public interest. There are also separate questions of state capacity in some of these polities and the fundamental ability of the government to recognize substantive problems and devise responses. Finally, external partners, particularly the United States, must recognize that the transactionalism of the moment will not deliver stability in one of the world’s most essential maritime corridors. The only solution is to encourage better and more accountable governance along Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden littoral.

    Industry News: Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival.
    • The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities.
    • It has been revealed that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Sources indicate that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    It has been revealed that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    “It began with the diesel deal. This is the longest sustained effort by Team Trump” to put its thumb on the scales, noted John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “It annoys me even more that they are helping [Russian President Vladimir] Putin do this. Putin wants to undermine NATO, and that is why it is so frustrating.”.

    Trump had previously adumbrated his approach to Ukraine by delaying approval of the bipartisan legislation, championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would have levied stiff tariffs on Russia’s trading partners and put additional sanctions on top Russian officials. When the legislation finally did pass, Trump watered it down, waiving the sanctions and for once forgetting about tariffs.

    It has been revealed that “I found U.S. policy over the last six weeks depressing,” said Steven Pifer, another former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “I think Trump is lost to the cause, even if the American people are not.”.

    In a recent development, now it falls to Europe to fill the gap, both in terms of Kyiv’s budget and its defense needs. About half of the latest loan is earmarked for Ukraine’s administration and the other half for defense procurement.

    The European loan is not a done deal. There are four holdouts among the usual suspects—Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic—that are leery of signing onto more blocwide debt to support a country they view askance. But by Friday, informed observers say, the European Union will probably be able to hammer through a fresh 45 billion on top of the 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine that it is still doling out.

    Sources indicate that european Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has remarked the latest loan would be backed by frozen Russian assets held in Europe. Those central bank assets total about $300 billion worldwide, with just over $200 billion in Belgium. Despite years of posturing, four years into the war, neither Europe nor the United States nor the United Kingdom has moved from freezing to seizing, fearful of the potential legal, financial, and other consequences of grabbing illicit Russian money. That makes the ultimate collateral for this newly introduced European loan something of a question mark.

    Industry observers note that “Europe has no choice but to fund Ukraine’s defense. The question is how you do it,” stated Timothy Ash, a Russia expert at Chatham House. “I find it incredible, when you put it across like this, which taxpayers should pay for this: Europe’s or Russia’s?” (He has some thoughts.).

    In a recent development, the bigger question is broader. Europe knows that enabling Ukraine to survive the war, or at least avoid a dishonorable peace, is critical to the country’s survival as well as its own. The problem, which has been apparent since January 2025, is that Ukraine and Europe are on their own. The United States has not provided any fresh financial support for Kyiv since Trump came back to office, has at times interrupted intelligence-sharing and satellite links, and continues to block the sale of much-need missile interceptors held in European inventories.

    U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby scolded Ukraine last week for striking Russian oil facilities, arguing that such attacks were ineffective. (Ukraine’s long-range strikes have taken offline about half of Russia’s refinery capacity in recent months, cratered its energy exports, and are leading to lines at gas stations in Russia.) Meanwhile, Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other major cities.

    “Trump is just defending Putin and making it harder for Ukraine to defend itself,” Herbst noted.

    Germany’s vocal support for mobilizing hundreds of billions of Moscow’s reserves could be a game-changer for Ukraine.

    For all the talk of a upcoming world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.

    Recent findings suggest that one question that looms now is whether Europe’s determination to support Ukraine—Europe has already provided nearly 240 billion euros (about $260 billion), far more than the United States or any other country—will push Trump into reprisal mode. He has in the past slapped tariffs on Europe while waiving penalties on Russia. Over the weekend, Trump posted a photo of himself with Putin titled, simply, “My Friend.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “If Trump wants to go down that route, it might get ugly in Europe, but I don’t think Europe can afford to let Ukraine lose. There is a real understanding in Europe about how high the stakes are for them,” Ash remarked.

    In a recent development, “It will be interesting to see where this goes in terms of the U.S.-EU relationship. This could be a huge crisis. We have to see how far he is willing to take this.”.

    #146620. Evidence sought by government spanned decades in Omar probe, upcoming records show

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (621 w)
